editorial_excerpt_zh: 纪念智证大师谥号1100年的特别展“国宝 三井寺之全部”将于明年4月20日至6月13日在东京国立博物馆平成馆（上野公园）举行。10月16日，该馆举办了记者发布会。天台寺门宗总本山园城寺（三井寺）……

article_text:
智証大師 諡号 1100年記念 特別展「国宝 三井寺のすべて」が東京国立博物館平成館（上野公園）で来年4月20日から6月13日まで開催されます。10月16日、同館で記者発表会が行われました。 天台寺門宗総本山である 園城寺 （ 三井寺 ）は、飛鳥時代に創建された滋賀県を代表する 古刹 です。智証大師 円珍 （814～891年）により天台別院として中興されて以来、幾多の戦乱に遭いながらも、復興により乗り越え、今日まで法灯を伝えてきました。

来年2027年は円珍が醍醐天皇により智証大師号を授かって1100年の節目にあたり、これを記念して、円珍ゆかりの寺宝の数々を一堂に公開する展覧会が開催されます。 記者発表では、国宝8件（「五部心観」（完本）（前欠本）、「不動明王像」（黄不動尊）、「過書」、「智証大師坐像」（御骨大師）、「智証大師坐像」（中尊大師）、「新羅明神坐像」、「円珍贈法印大和尚位並智証大師諡号勅書」など）、重要文化財42件など約80件が公開されると発表されました。なお巡回はありません。

みどころとして次の4点が強調されました。

①三井寺とその礎を築いた名僧・円珍を紹介するおよそ20年ぶりの展覧会 ​② 現存最古のパスポート（過所）をはじめとした貴重な円珍文書を公開 ​③ 狩野永徳の長男、光信の傑作「勧学院客殿障壁画」を再現展示 ​④ めったにお目にかかれない三井寺の秘仏が集結

後日詳しくプレビューします。（読売新聞美術展ナビ編集班 岡本公樹）

智証大師諡号1100年記念 特別展「国宝 三井寺のすべて」

会場：東京国立博物館 平成館（東京都台東区上野公園13-9）

会期：2027年4月20日（火）～6月13日（日） 【前期】4月20日（火）～5月16日（日） 【後期】5月18日（火）～6月13日（日）

開館時間：9時30分～17時00分 ※毎週金・土曜日および5月2日（日・祝）、5月3日（月・祝）、5月4日（火・祝）は20時00分まで開館 ※入館は閉館の30分前まで

休館日：月曜日※ただし4月26日、5月3日、5月31日、6月7日は開館（5月31日、6月7日は本展のみ開館。東博コレクション展は休館日のため観覧不可）

問い合わせ：050-5541-8600（ハローダイヤル、午前9時～午後8時） 詳細は、 展覧会公式サイト まで。

article_text:
This week and next, Film Comment is reporting from the picturesque shores of the Lido, where the Venice Film Festival takes place each year. This year’s edition features new films by many major auteurs, including Werner Herzog, Lee Chang-dong, Tsai Ming-liang, and more.

To kick off our coverage, Film Comment Co-Editor Devika Girish invited critics Miriam Bale and Öykü Sofuoğlu to discuss some of the most highly anticipated premieres of the festival’s first days, including Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine (2:45), Werner Herzog’s Bucking Fastard (10:10), Paul Schrader’s The Basics of Philosophy (22:06), and Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime (31:52).

Subscribe today to Film Comment to stay up-to-date with all of our Venice 2026 coverage.

title_original: Sophie Calle. L’amore, la morte e altre forme di sopravvivenza
editorial_title_zh: Sophie Calle：爱、死亡与其他生存形式
editorial_excerpt_zh: 在罗马MAXXI（国立二十一世纪艺术博物馆），这场献给这位法国艺术家的意大利最大规模个人回顾展汇集了跨越八个项目的约450件作品。在婚礼、离异与葬礼之间，这是一场关于记忆与执念的探究，它挑战了经验、虚构与……之间的界限
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "死亡比生者有一个优势：它不再需要为自己辩解。它不作承诺，不搞背叛，也不改变主意。如果要说的话，反倒是幸存者不得不去处理那些令人尴尬的缺席管理工作：保留照片、盘点物品、守护那些再也没有人能反驳的话语。苏菲·卡尔（Sophie Calle）将这种执着变成了一种艺术实践。她不作安慰，不予救赎，也从不奢望归还那些已经失去的东西。相反，她将痛苦置于一种近乎官僚主义的纪律之下，去衡量它、编目它、将其展出。她的天才之处在于将执念转化为一种方法，把自己的生存变成了一场不一定知道结果的实验。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": Antonacci）策展的个人回顾展。大约450件展品分布在从1978年到2026年的八个项目中，构成了一条非时间顺序的参观路线，与卡尔共同构思为大型装置艺术。甚至连伴随各个展区的文字也出自她的手笔。因此，博物馆放弃了惯常的说明性中介，将叙事的掌控权也交给了艺术家。这一选择与其诗学保持一致，但并非没有含混之处：当创作者同时掌控作品及其阐释时，留给观众去反驳的空间还有多少？", "links": "这些最早拍摄于1978年、位于加利福尼亚州波利纳斯墓地的照片，拍摄了刻有“Brother”（兄弟）和“Sister”（姐妹）等字样的墓碑。在《Le tombe》（墓穴）中，身份通过定义它的纽带得以存续。她的核心研究已经显现：并非死亡本身，而是那些在消逝之后依然存在的事物。卡尔似乎对最终事件本身的兴趣，远不及对它在留下之人的意识中那顽固持久状态的兴趣。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "说到底，婚姻或许是我们所有葬礼中最乐观的一种。它庆祝一种无人知晓其期限的情感的永恒性。两个人向对方许下无法保证的诺言，面对着那些被请来证明意图之真诚而非其未来实现的证人。在卡尔的作品中，婚礼也变成了一种表象，正如在《Double Blind》中所呈现的那样，这是她与格雷格·谢帕德（Greg article_text:
La morte ha un vantaggio sui vivi: non deve più giustificarsi. Non promette, non tradisce, non cambia idea. Sono i sopravvissuti, semmai, a doversi occupare dell’imbarazzante amministrazione dell’assenza: conservare fotografie, inventariare oggetti, custodire parole che nessuno potrà più smentire. Sophie Calle ha fatto di questa ostinazione una pratica artistica. Non consola, non redime, non pretende di restituire ciò che è perduto. Sottopone piuttosto il dolore a una disciplina quasi burocratica, lo misura, lo cataloga, lo espone. La sua genialità consiste nell’aver trasformato l’ossessione in un metodo, facendo della propria esistenza un esperimento del quale non conosce necessariamente il risultato.

È questa la contraddizione che attraversa Matrimoni, Rotture e Funerali inclusi , la monografica che il MAXXI dedica all’artista francese, a cura di Simona Antonacci . Circa 450 elementi, distribuiti in otto progetti dal 1978 al 2026, compongono un percorso non cronologico, concepito insieme a Calle come una grande installazione. Persino i testi che accompagnano le sezioni appartengono alla sua scrittura. Il museo rinuncia così alla consueta mediazione didascalica per affidare all’artista anche il controllo del racconto. Una scelta coerente con la sua poetica, ma non priva di ambiguità: quando l’autore governa contemporaneamente l’opera e la sua interpretazione, quanto spazio rimane allo spettatore per contraddirlo?

Le prime fotografie, realizzate nel 1978 nel cimitero californiano di Bolinas, ritraggono lapidi con iscrizioni come Brother e Sister . In Le tombe , l’identità sopravvive attraverso i legami che l’hanno definita. È già presente il nucleo della sua ricerca: non la morte in sé, ma ciò che continua a esistere dopo la scomparsa. Calle sembra interessata meno all’evento conclusivo che alla sua ostinata permanenza nella coscienza di chi resta.

Il matrimonio, del resto, è forse il più ottimista dei nostri riti funebri. Celebra l’eternità di un sentimento del quale nessuno conosce la durata. Due persone si promettono ciò che non possono garantire, davanti a testimoni chiamati a certificare la sincerità di un’intenzione, non la sua futura realizzazione. Nella produzione di Calle, anche le nozze diventano rappresentazione, come in Double Blind , realizzato con Greg Shephard durante un viaggio negli Stati Uniti culminato in un matrimonio a Las Vegas. Due persone, due videocamere, due versioni della stessa esperienza. La promessa matrimoniale diventa un documento, non una garanzia. E l’amore, sottoposto alla prova della rappresentazione, rivela quanto sia difficile distinguere ciò che viviamo dalla storia che desideriamo raccontarne.

In Funerali inclusi , fotografie e testi costruiscono un’autobiografia nella quale la verità non viene necessariamente falsificata, ma sottoposta a un regime di selezione. Calle decide cosa ricordare, cosa esporre e cosa lasciare nell’ombra. Non è una semplice operazione narrativa: è un esercizio di potere sulla memoria. L’artista diventa contemporaneamente testimone, protagonista e giudice della propria esistenza. Ma chi racconta possiede davvero ciò che racconta? E soprattutto, quale diritto esercita sulle persone che entrano nella sua storia? È in questa zona moralmente instabile che la ricerca di Calle raggiunge la propria radicalità. L’intimità cessa di essere un territorio protetto e diventa materia pubblica, mentre il documento fotografico, anziché garantire la verità, ne rivela l’insufficienza.

Questa tensione attraversa anche L’Hôtel , il progetto nel quale, lavorando come cameriera in un albergo veneziano, fotografa gli oggetti lasciati dagli ospiti nelle camere. Proprio l’acquisizione di un’opera di questa serie ha contribuito ad avviare il dialogo tra l’artista e il MAXXI. L’indagine assume qui i caratteri di un’ossessione metodica: osservare, catalogare, ricostruire esistenze sconosciute attraverso i loro residui materiali. Ma il controllo produce informazioni, non necessariamente conoscenza. L’altro può essere osservato indefinitamente senza cessare di essere uno sconosciuto. E la curiosità, quando diventa sistematica, non è sempre innocente.

In Dolore squisito , nucleo centrale dell’esposizione con circa 230 elementi, la fine di una relazione diventa un esperimento sulla sofferenza. Calle organizza un conto alla rovescia verso l’abbandono e successivamente ripete il proprio racconto, confrontandolo con i dolori degli altri. La ripetizione assume quasi la funzione di un rituale: tornare sull’evento traumatico fino a modificarne il significato. È una psicologia dell’ossessione priva di qualsiasi compiacimento terapeutico. Non sappiamo se l’arte possa guarire dall’abbandono. Certamente può sottrarre a chi abbandona il monopolio della narrazione.

La morte biologica interviene come espressione estrema della medesima indagine. In Non ho potuto catturare la morte , Calle filma gli ultimi istanti della madre, tentando inutilmente di registrarne l’ultimo respiro. La tecnologia può documentare un corpo, non possedere il momento in cui la vita lo abbandona. Che cosa significa trasformare l’agonia in un’immagine? Dove termina la testimonianza e comincia l’appropriazione artistica del dolore? Calle non cerca riparo nella solennità del lutto. E l’arte, evidentemente, non è tenuta a comportarsi come una buona parente al capezzale di un morente.

In Polo Nord , invece, seppellisce in un ghiacciaio una fotografia della madre e alcuni gioielli, realizzandone simbolicamente il desiderio di raggiungere l’Artico. Il lutto diventa un rito, la perdita una geografia affettiva. Anche il Catalogo ragionato dell’incompiuto partecipa a questa economia dell’assenza: progetti abbandonati, idee interrotte e tentativi falliti vengono ordinati in un inventario del possibile. Non tutto ciò che muore ha avuto il tempo di esistere. E ciò che non è accaduto può continuare a esercitare sulla coscienza un potere maggiore di ciò che abbiamo realmente vissuto.

In Perché , fotografie nascoste dietro tende ricamate vengono svelate dal visitatore, mentre le parole raccontano non ciò che le immagini rappresentano, ma le ragioni che hanno spinto l’artista a realizzarle. Fuori dal museo, al Cimitero Acattolico di Roma, una nuova opera del 2026 accoglie invece i segreti affidati a Calle. Non sono più soltanto i morti a essere sepolti, ma le parole dei vivi. Il segreto trova una tomba prima ancora del suo proprietario. È un gesto insieme poetico e spietato, perché suggerisce che ciascuno di noi custodisca qualcosa che preferirebbe vedere scomparire prima di sé.

A concludere il percorso è Voir la mer , videoinstallazione realizzata a Istanbul nel 2011, dove Calle accompagna al mare persone che, pur vivendo vicino alla costa, non lo avevano mai visto. Dopo matrimoni, abbandoni, funerali e fallimenti, compare qualcosa di inatteso: la meraviglia. L’artista che sembrava ossessionata dalla scomparsa costruisce finalmente un’occasione di presenza. Ma anche qui resta una domanda: la meraviglia appartiene a chi la prova o a chi decide di trasformarla in un’immagine?

Sophie Calle non ha inventato un’estetica del lutto. Ha costruito una spietata grammatica della sopravvivenza, nella quale amare, perdere e ricordare sono operazioni meno distanti di quanto vorremmo credere. Il matrimonio promette l’eternità, la separazione ne denuncia l’imprudenza, il funerale ne celebra l’impossibilità. Ma dopo la morte, dopo il fallimento e dopo l’abbandono, rimane ancora qualcosa da vedere. Forse persino il mare, per la prima volta.

article_text:
Quentin Tarantino surprised audiences on Friday night at AFI Fest when he shared the first 17 minutes of “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”

Tarantino made a special appearance at the TCL Chinese Theatre in Hollywood, following a screening of “Once Upon a Time … In Hollywood.” Following the Q&A moderated by Rotten Tomatoes’ Jacqueline Coley, the filmmaker said, “Well, I could talk a little bit about ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ or I could show you the first 17 minutes.”

Related Stories

Directed by David Fincher , who was also in attendance, the film sees the return of Cliff Booth played by Brad Pitt. The film picks up in 1977 from the original film’s 1969 timeline. The logline reads: “Los Angeles no longer needs a hippie-slaying stuntman the way it did. But Hollywood will always have problems, problems that can only be solved by someone with Cliff’s unique (occasionally extralegal) abilities. When he’s not earning his keep bartending or as a projectionist, Cliff Booth is a fixer — solving situations for Hollywood’s great and, sometimes, not so good.”

Popular on Variety

He’s curious when he gets a call from talent agent Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), on behalf of her client, TV megastar Charlie Peters (Scott Caan) — a man known for doing his own stunts. And he’s further entertained and intrigued when he meets other characters in Charlie’s world, from his knowing wife Toni (Carla Gugino) to pro football champion turned screen star Roderick “Hot Rod” Harrison (Yahya Abdul-Mateen II). Then there are the Verdusco brothers (Matt Groove and JB Tadena), mysterious gangsters causing mayhem across the city. What was once a fairytale is now a crime story — a cocktail of violence, ambition and desire that could only happen in LA.

Tarantino, who wrote the screenplay, shared his decision to revisit Cliff Booth. He said, “I tend to not remember good reviews of mine in quotes; I remember the bad reviews in quotes, but I don’t really remember good reviews of mine in quotes. But one quote that I do remember somebody writing about ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ was, ‘This seems like the first world Quentin Tarantino has ever created that he would like to live in’ and there is that aspect; I loved the Cliff Booth character,” Tarantino said. “I loved the way that Brad played him, and there was this aspect of him as sort of like a paperback hero. I could see like a series of paperbacks with Cliff Booth getting involved with this adventure or that adventure or something like that.”

While further plot details can’t be spoiled, the opening sequence has Tarantino’s distinguished style of writing and visually, the Hollywood of 1977 is, in true Fincher style, gritty and dark.

The Netflix film also stars Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Carla Gugino, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II and Peter Weller and is set to premiere in Imax theaters on Nov. 25, before hitting the streamer Dec. 23.

The evening kicked off with Tarantino introducing the film and shared that had not seen the film at that theater.

In the Q&A, Tarantino shared how he had spoken with Burt Reynolds about playing the George Spahn character. Tarantino recalled, “He said yes and we became friendly, but he passed away before we could make the film. But we did get to rehearse with him and do the script reading with him, so actually, the last performance Burt Reynolds ever gave was as George Spahn in the script reading.”

The character would be played by Bruce Dern.

He also talked about his upcoming play “The Popinjay Cavalier ,” which stars Sacha Baron Cohen and is set to premiere in London’s West End next year. “I’m not going to talk a whole lot about that, but our previews are in February. In November we’ll start rehearsals.” He went on to say, “I’m just a writer and that’s just kind of what I do. I’m always writing.”

article_text:
Though he is the designated newcomer of the “ Behemoth! ” Music Collective, composer and songwriter Lukas Frank has a level of familiarity with its director that makes him one of the few people that can say they did rewrites on something two-time Oscar nominee Tony Gilroy wrote.

Speaking at the Middleburg Film Festival after a Sunday morning screening of the Pedro Pascal vehicle that features music from nine different composers, Gilroy said, “Lukas and I have a relationship that goes back like 10 years. His father [Scott] and I are very good friends and Lukas was a real touring drummer.” Over the years, the filmmaker had stayed in touch with the burgeoning musician, and became a fan of Frank’s band Storefront Church, “so we had a real relationship. I know his music inside out.” But even then, as Gilroy began working on “Behemoth!,” he said that Frank “wasn’t really going to be part of it originally. It wasn’t like he was an obvious choice.”

As Gilroy developed ideas for what music could be featured in the film in order to avoid an underscore, from Oscar winner Michael Giacchino writing the theme to a fictional classic cartoon to music icon Alan Silvestri scoring a blockbuster titled “Open World,” the biggest challenge actually became what music represented the character Viviana, a young woman who Pascal’s professional cellist character Alan Serian takes interest in.

“It says on the page, oh, it’s this transformational [requiem], this woman beyond a prodigy, a proto-Mozart,” describing one of the pieces that first showcases the young musician’s talent. “It’s like when a writer says, ‘Oh, the greatest sunset ever.’ The director goes, ‘Fuck you. Really?’ So I’m on both sides of that equation, but I know that I have to have this thing, and I just know intuitively that this is going to be the hardest thing to do. So I started very early on.”

Gilroy cast a wide net that finally came back around to a piece that his primary music collaborator, nine-time Oscar nominee James Newton Howard , wrote. “We picked a lock on the Viviana thing,” said the director. “At that point I said, ‘Oh, my God, James, you know what? Now that you have the genetics of this, now that we know who this is, you should take the rest of the Viviana cues.’ He destroyed them. I love what he does with Viviana.”

One of those cues was an original song called “Your God Is Sleeping,” an experimental pop song that Pascal’s Alex sees Viviana perform at a packed music club in Los Angeles. “I wrote a version of it and brought it to James. He tweaked it up and had all the lyrics. We’re like ‘Wow, this is kind of good. We should take it over to Lukas and have him make a hit,’” said Gilroy. “Lukas listens to it and goes, ‘It’s really good, but it’s really old.’”

Seated next to the “Behemoth!” helmer, Frank said “Tony wrote this great song, it felt like a ‘70s protest song.” “It wasn’t that lame,” replied Gilroy.

“It was a good song. It did not feel like something a 16-year-old girl could write was my complaint about it,” said the songwriter. The director said, “‘OK, you can have the title. Do whatever you want.’ And then a couple of days later the song came out.”

“Your God Is Sleeping” served as redemption for Frank who had sent Gilroy several pitches for the aforementioned pivotal piece of music that a younger Viviana performs in the film. “All along the way, Lukas is like, ‘What are you doing? What happened? What’s going on? Let me try.’ He tried a bunch of Viviana requiems and kept sending them to me, but our relationship is different. I can just say ‘No, no, no, no, no, no, no, no. Don’t stop, but no. Forget it. I don’t see how this is going to happen,’” said the director.

“Someday I’m going to release my four projected piano requiems. I got such great feedback,” joked Frank. “My favorite one, the piece was called ‘My Mother.’ Tony had the title for me, he wanted me to call it ‘My Mother.’ So I sent him one of them. I’m so proud of this piano requiem I sent. I sent it over to him. He goes, ‘I mean, it’s great. I’m sure your mother will love it.’”

After laughter from the audience, the composer continued, “I sent him another one over and he goes, ‘This is the definition of interesting for interesting’s sake.’ I then put that song [and melody] on my record. I don’t tell him. I send it to him. He goes, ‘Track four is great.’ I go ‘Motherfucker! That’s the one that you said wasn’t that good.’”

“Behemoth!” is a cornucopia of engrossing, original music, and Gilroy said Howard, the victor in the hunt for who would write music for Viviana, “was obsessed with what Lukas was doing after ‘Your God Is Sleeping.’” He added that part of the fun of the film’s musical experiment was “all the composers on this movie wanted to hear what the other ones were doing,” and they all thought Best Original Song contender “Your God Is Sleeping” “is the dopest. It’s really hard to be that simple and that effective. It’s really cool.”
excerpt_original: Composer Lukas Frank called Tony Gilroy's version of the “Behemoth!" original song “Your God Is Sleeping” a "’70s protest song." “It wasn't that lame,” joked the director at the Middleburg Film Festival.

"正是柯蒂斯，让普露（字面意义上）撞上了他——当时她违背父母意愿，把婴儿弟弟麦克带到了市中心；也是柯蒂斯在场时，一群电脑生成的乌鸦（鉴于其数量，简直是一场屠杀）把麦克抱起，飞向威拉麦河对岸的森林。“世界上有些地方，人们注定永远不该涉足，”麦克先生一向是这么评价那片森林的。果不其然，普露和柯蒂斯刚骑着自行车穿过雾气蒙蒙的铁轨，就被一只极具法西斯色彩、会说话的土狼（由汤姆·威茨配音）缠上了，它是某位因悲伤而发狂的太后女伯爵亚历山德拉（凯瑞·穆里根饰）招募的众多动物中最忠诚的一员，而亚历山德拉正执意对该王国发动她那场前途未卜的战争。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她是想统治这片“不可逾越之森”，还是想将其毁灭？她的意图和她的执行计划一样扑朔迷离（这计划似乎与控制某种具有自我意识且强大的常春藤品种有关），但更重要的是，亚历山德拉那疯狂的悲情色彩让她集贾尼斯、《指环王》中的萨鲁曼以及《白雪公主》中的邪恶王后于一身：她的痛苦将她对已故儿子曾经的特殊之爱，变质为一种更寻常的执念——一心想要欺骗死亡，或者至少将其掌控在自己手中。穆里根用每一个带着毒刺的词句将这位女伯爵的心碎与疯狂演绎得淋漓尽致，然而这个角色在悲伤五阶段之间的挣扎，却被深埋在一个同样难以驾驭自身执念的奇幻传奇之中。", "《荒野林》是一场规模空前的视觉饕餮盛宴，达到了莱卡工作室从未尝试过的高度，但其设计的精妙与密度反倒衬托出其叙事之平庸。尽管这部电影由于凝聚了极多的心血而远未彻底沦为平庸之作，但当柯蒂斯和普露分开之后（他被迫在太后女伯爵的军队中作战，而她则被她向其求助的人类官僚囚禁），一种眩晕般的不适感便油然而生，因为注入每一帧画面的非凡才华极少延伸到他们两人之间的化学反应上。", "translated": {"type": "paragraph", "text": "除此之外，《荒野林》对御用配音演员查理·戴和奥卡菲娜的使用，比他们以往参演的大多数动画电影要略微惊艳一些，但人们很难摆脱这样一种感觉：莱卡工作室迄今为止最具野心的项目，同时也是在借鉴《超级马力欧银河大电影》和《愤怒的小鸟2》的套路来给自己留退路。一部电影难免如此——其女主角和工作室都在艰难地试图弥合孩童心态与成人关切之间的鸿沟，然而除了这些元文本式的花招之外，几乎没有什么能帮助塑造普露的自我发现之旅，这一旅程最终被她在途中遇到的列队成行的受魔法影响的树木、友好的老鼠和可怕的战士们稀释成了冗长乏味之物。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "全世界所有的3D打印面孔也无法阻止这些角色流露出扁平感，而该片为了将梅洛的小说塞进一个时长达131分钟的故事而做出的种种勉强努力，迫使莱卡及其团队做出了妥协，而《荒野林》唯有靠其丰富的奇观才能勉强支撑。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尽管柯蒂斯作为联合主角有着充足的银幕时间，但他毫无疑问仍是这些妥协中最明显的牺牲品；虽然他作为普露那鲁莽早熟性格的平衡对照显得合情合理，但他自身的存在也从未被赋予太多合理的动机。一部更成熟的电影，或者至少是一部更能探索“坚守与放手”这一终身博弈的电影，本可以把普露的妈妈（玛雅·厄斯金饰）和爸爸推向台前——在剧情过半处的一个转折让这对父母自身与魔法思维的关系变得扑朔迷离之后，本可顺理成章地挖掘下去，然而就连这个重磅的情节反转在这样一部电影里也显得有些哑火，这部电影和麦克尔夫妇一样，在想象与现实的平衡上举步维艰——它极力想要兼顾方程的两端，最终却两边都没能做到极致。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "莱卡标志性的定格动画既具有触感，又依赖于幻觉的巫术，是将其挣扎转化为艺术的理想媒介。或许正因如此，该工作室如今对电脑特效的依赖——通过与Wētā FX合作实现——与其说是解决普露危机的方案，倒不如说是她危机的一种症状。该片2,804个镜头中有670个经过了CGI特效增强，其中许多镜头明显得让人无法忽视。这并不是因为特效过于刺眼（其中许多特效被无缝融入了莱卡标志性的视觉风格中），而是因为这种效果是不可能的。片中的数字环境、大炮轰鸣、列队的土狼军队以及直冲云霄的野生常春藤之墙，统统违背了人类双手所能企及的极限，以至于该片最震撼的场景由于其创作过程的诡异感而大打折扣。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当然，这只是部分而言。正如勇气并不意味着没有恐惧，长大成人也并不意味着抛弃童年惊叹的所有痕迹，一个老套的故事和一些数字点缀并不代表《野木森林》不是一部值得细细品味的罕见奇观，也不代表莱卡不知所措地迷失了方向。事实上，这部电影似乎近乎刻意地迎合了这些瑕疵，仿佛是为了让观众专注于欣赏那些在瑕疵中幸存下来的美。正如一位饱经沧桑的角色对普鲁所说的那样：“你总是执着于在世界上看不到任何魔法，却在每一片草叶和绽放的花朵中与它擦肩而过。”观看一部莱卡电影，哪怕是——或者说尤其是——这部电影，就是要在你目之所及的每一处重新发现这种魔法。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "评级：B-", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《野木森林》在2026年伦敦电影节上首映。Fathom Entertainment将于10月23日周三在院线发行该片。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on October 11, 2026 at the 2026 London Film Festival. Fathom Entertainment will release the film in theaters on Wednesday, October 21.]

On the one hand, Travis Knight’s “ Wildwood ” is an epic, eye-popping, and almost unfathomably well-crafted celebration of everything that makes Laika special — of everything that makes the Oregon-based stop-motion studio a singular force for good in a film industry where most companies are less interested in savoring the magic of animation than they are in seeing how many shortcuts they can take without breaking its spell. On the other hand, the remarkable time and care that went into “Wildwood” doesn’t prevent it from being the least enchanting of Laika ’s films, even if its flaws help to reinforce the power of a story about how magic can persist in spite of itself.

The longest and most ambitious movie of its kind ever made, this sprawling fantasy saga about the overlap between reality and imagination — about a teenage girl in the Pacific Northwest who ventures into an enchanted kingdom to rescue her toddler little brother after he’s abducted there by a murder of crows — pushes the form to new extremes at a time when the rest of the business is hoping that audiences will learn to settle for less. It’s a mad feat of muchness.

Laika 3D-printed 142,000 different face models, hand-molded 728 individual trees, and used more than 715 miles of brass wire across 1,155 days of production. They created a “Braveheart”-style battle one frame at a time, built a perfect miniature replica of Powell’s City of Books to bring the movie’s version of Portland to life (complete with a Drag Queen Story Hour sign), and even designed tiny little Decemberists posters to adorn the heroine’s living room; she seems to be more of a fan of their post-“The Crane Wife” output, but I’m trying my best not to hold that against her.

That degree of loving attention comes at a massive price, of course (with one negligible exception, each of Laika’s films has cost more and grossed less than the one before it), but studio owner and Nike co-founder Phil Knight can certainly afford it, and it doesn’t hurt that his son is running the shop. Not all Hollywood nepo babies! In lieu of any prolonged fawning over the pursuits of a billionaire heir, let’s just say the Skydance merger would probably seem a bit less cataclysmic if David Ellison were capable of directing something as artful and transcendent as “ Kubo and the Two Strings ” (or even something as competent and colorful as last summer’s live-action “Masters of the Universe,” for that matter).

Which is all to say that “Wildwood” epitomizes why Laika should be treated like a national treasure: It’s stunning, it’s sincere, it’s possessed by a combination of American moxie and a Ghibli-esque willingness to push young audiences out of their comfort zones, and it’s seemingly at peace with losing enough money to sink any other animation studio on the planet. It is, in so many respects, the ultimate testament to what makes Laika unique. It’s also, in so many others, the first of their movies that doesn’t feel as special as it looks (and sometimes doesn’t look as special as it should feel).

Appropriately enough for a project that suggests Laika’s care may not be enough to preserve its magic, “Wildwood” is a story about losing faith in the wonder of the world. And appropriately enough for a project that still has so much to offer in spite of its flaws, “Wildwood” is also a story about how magic can persist in our lives even after we stop believing in it — even after its child-like purity gives way to something mottled and imperfect.

It’s a story that Knight and Laika’s go-to screenwriter Chris Butler have adapted from the 2011 novel of the same name by Decemberists frontman Colin Meloy, and from the Carson Ellis illustrations that brought that book to life. (Ellis is Meloy’s wife, and her album art is as crucial to the Decemberists’ identity as any of their early songs about castaways, cutouts, and homesick legionnaires.) The drawings were extraordinary, but the text — while unsurprisingly playful — was also tropey and wanting, and the wanting came in waves.

The visuals are exponentially more expansive and nuanced in this “Wildwood.” The writing is not. It is often charming though. It is dark. Very dark. Even by the standards of the animation studio behind “Coraline” and “Paranorman.” (Parents should be advised that the PG-13 rating is there for a reason from the first scene, even though I suspect this film will be broadly enjoyable for most older kids.) And, for a time, it is obviously — inimitably — the work of Laika, if only because no other studio would ever love Portland this much.

Teenage Prue McKeel (Peyton Elizabeth Lee), however, seems kind of over the hippie Never-never Land of it all. She rolls her eyes at her dad’s plant collection, and his juvenile bedtime stories about the “Impassable Wilderness” on the other side of The St. John’s Bridge, and probably also his beloved red beanie when he isn’t looking. (Mr. McKeel is voiced by a sweetly pained Jake Johnson.) Prue barely even acknowledges the guy riding a unicycle past her local coffee shop while playing the bagpipes from under a Darth Vader mask. It’s time for her to put childlike things aside. Things like her underdeveloped friendship with the nerdy Curtis Mehlberg (Jacob Tremblay), a lovably round-faced dork who’s still obsessed with playing tabletop fantasy games where he pretends to be a hero.

It’s Curtis who Prue (literally) bumps into when she takes her baby brother Mac downtown against her parents’ wishes, and it’s Curtis who’s there when a murder of computer-generated crows — more like a massacre , given their numbers — scoop Mac up and fly him toward the forest on the other side of the Willamette River. “There are places in the world people were never meant to go,” is what Mr. McKeel has always said about those woods, and sure enough Prue and Curtis have barely just biked there across the foggy train tracks before they’re beset upon by a fascistic talking coyote voiced by Tom Waits, the most loyal of the many animals that a grief-mad dowager governess named Alexandra (Carey Mulligan) has conscripted into her uncertain war against the realm.

Does she want to rule the Impassable Woods, or does she want to destroy them? Her intentions remain as difficult to parse as her plan for executing them (which has something to do with seizing control over a sentient and powerful breed of ivy), but it’s more important that Alexandra’s demented pathos allows her to be Jadis, Sarumon, and the Evil Queen from “Snow White” all at once, as her pain has soured the special love she felt for her late son into a more generic fixation with cheating death, or at least commanding it under her control. Mulligan sells the governess’ heartbreak and madness with every poison-tipped word, but her character’s struggle to negotiate between the five stages of grief is entombed within a fantasy saga that has a similarly hard time of harnessing its obsessions.

“Wildwood” is a mind-boggling visual smorgasbord on a scale that Laika has never attempted before, but the brilliance and density of its design can’t help but call attention to the ordinariness of its storytelling. While the movie is far too lovingly crafted to ever flatline altogether, a vertiginous discomfort kicks in after Curtis and Prue are split up (he’s forced to fight in the dowager governess’ army, while she’s imprisoned by the human bureaucrats she asks for help), as the singular genius infused into each frame seldom extends to the alchemy between them.

Individual sequences are incredible, Prue’s escape from the bureaucrats’ mansion chief among them, every new detail we learn about the Impassable Woods — and every new creature we meet within them — makes the film’s world seem less worthy of Laika’s painstaking attention. I adored the flamboyantly theatrical Owl Rex (instant “Celebrity Traitors” legend Richard E. Grant), and then felt betrayed that his only purpose was to establish Alexandra’s backstory. I was delighted to hear Mahershala Ali in the role of a bandit king named Brendan, and then disappointed that his character is reduced to a stock archetype in the fight against Alexandra.

Elsewhere, “Wildwood” makes slightly more surprising use of go-to voice actors Charlie Day and Awkwafina than most of the many animated movies they’ve been slotted into before, but it’s hard to shake the sense that Laika’s most ambitious project so far is also hedging its bets by stealing a page from “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie” and “Angry Birds 2.” So it goes in a film whose heroine — and whose studio — are both struggling to bridge the gap between kid sensibilities and more adult concerns, and yet there’s little beyond such meta-textual flourishes to help shape Prue’s journey of self-discovery, which is diluted into tedium by the parade of enchanted trees, friendly rats, and fearsome warriors she meets along the way.

All the 3D-printed faces in the world can’t stop these characters from feeling two-dimensional, and the film’s strained efforts to fit Meloy’s novel into the stuff of an 131-minute story force Knight and co. to make compromises that “Wildwood” can only survive on the strength of its abundant wonder.

Despite his ample screentime as a co-lead, Curtis is nevertheless the most obvious victim of those compromises; while he makes sense as a counterweight to Prue’s headlong precociousness, he’s also never given much of his own reason to exist. A more adult film, or at least one more capable of exploring the life-long negotiation between holding on and letting go might have brought Prue’s mom (Maya Erskine) and dad to the fore after a mid-story revelation complicates their own relationship with magical thinking, but even that bombshell plot twist proves something of a dud in a movie that shares the McKeels’ struggle to split the difference between imagination and reality — a movie that strains to honor both sides of the equation, and ultimately serves neither to their fullest extent.

As tactile as it is dependent upon the sorcery of illusion, Laika’s brand of stop-motion animation is the ideal medium for transmuting that struggle into art. Perhaps that’s why the studio’s new reliance upon computer trickery — courtesy of a collaboration with Wētā FX — feels more like more of a symptom of Prue’s crisis than part of the solution to it. 670 of the movie’s 2,804 shots have been augmented by CGI, many of them too obviously to ignore. That’s not because the effects work is glaringly obvious (much of it is seamlessly woven into Laika’s signature look), but rather because it’s impossible. The film’s digital environments, cannon explosions, marching coyote armies, and soaring walls of wild ivy all fly in the face of what human hands can do, to the point that the movie’s most impressive scenes are partially deflated by the uncanniness of their creation.

Only partially, of course. Just as courage doesn’t mean the absence of fear, and growing up doesn’t mean leaving every trace of childhood astonishment behind, a trite story and a few digital embellishments don’t mean that “Wildwood” isn’t a rare spectacle worth savoring, or that Laika has somehow lost its way. Indeed, the film almost seems to deliberately court these defects, as if to focus its audience on appreciating the beauty that survives them. As one particularly wizened character tells Prue it: “You’re so intent on seeing no magic in the world, but you miss it in every blade of grass and budding flower.” To watch a Laika movie, even — or especially — this one, is to rediscover that magic everywhere you look.

Grade: B-

“Wildwood” premiered at the 2026 London Film Festival. Fathom Entertainment will release it Wednesday, October 23 in theaters.

article_text:
Artists, collectives, researchers and curators worldwide are invited to apply for the Art Explora and Cité internationale des arts Residency Programme in Paris, France, offering funded opportunities to explore the intersections of art, science, technology and contemporary social and ecological challenges.

Open Call:

Art Explora has announced its 2027 residency programme in partnership with Cité internationale des arts, inviting international artists, collectives, researchers and curators to develop projects that investigate relationships between artistic practice, scientific enquiry and technological innovation.

The programme encourages interdisciplinary approaches to contemporary social and ecological questions, giving participants time, space, and resources to advance their creative and research practices.

Two residency formats are available:

SOLO Programme: Designed exclusively for individual artists.

COLLECTIVE Programme: Open to artist collectives or collaborations between artists and researchers or curators.

Residencies run for three or six months, with two sessions scheduled between March 2027 and February 2028.

Institutional Context:

Established in 2021, the Art Explora residency programme in Paris supports artistic research and experimentation while fostering connections between artists, cultural professionals and audiences.

Since its inception, the programme has welcomed more than 145 residents from 58 countries, representing diverse artistic disciplines, generations and cultural backgrounds.

The initiative forms part of Art Explora’s broader commitment to developing encounters between art and audiences at local, national and international levels.

Through its partnership with Cité internationale des arts, the programme provides access to dedicated creative spaces in Paris alongside curatorial guidance, production support, mentorship and professional networking opportunities.

Eligibility and Criteria:

Applications are open to artists, artist collectives, researchers and curators from around the world, subject to the requirements of the selected residency format.

Eligible artistic disciplines include:

Visual arts

Performing arts

Digital arts

Eligible research fields include:

Humanities

Social sciences

Sciences

Technological innovation

Ecology

Proposed projects should explore connections between art, science and technology while engaging with contemporary social or ecological issues.

The SOLO Programme is reserved for individual artists, while the COLLECTIVE Programme accommodates collaborative artistic practices and partnerships involving artists, researchers and curators.

Evaluation Process:

The programme seeks proposals that engage with its interdisciplinary focus and address contemporary questions through artistic or research-based approaches.

The On the Move announcement does not detail specific assessment criteria, jury composition, or selection procedures. Applicants should consult the official Art Explora application guidelines for further information about the selection process.

Practical Information:

Application deadline: 30 October 2026

Location: Cité internationale des arts, Montmartre, Paris, France

Residency duration: Three or six months

Residency sessions:

Session 1: March to August 2027

Session 2: September 2027 to February 2028

Each resident receives:

A fully furnished and equipped live-work studio of approximately 50 m².

A monthly living allowance of €1,000.

A production grant of €3,000.

Round-trip travel to Paris.

Curatorial and production support throughout the residency.

Access to mentorship and professional networking opportunities.

The programme offers participants the opportunity to develop their practices in an international creative environment while building connections across artistic and research disciplines.

Applications and Queries:

Submit applications by 30 October 2026 through the official Art Explora application platform.

Applicants should consult the programme’s official guidelines for submission requirements, supporting documentation and any additional conditions applicable to their chosen residency format.

Programme information and applications: Art Explora Residency Programme

Additional information: On the Move, Residency Programme 2027

article_text:
Andy Warhol famously said that in the future, everyone will have 15 minutes of fame. “Trust Me, I’m A Doctor” expands that tally to an hour and 51 minutes for Sandeep Kapoor, the physician who treated Playboy Playmate Anna Nicole Smith and was implicated in her death from a prescription drug overdose in 2007. That’s too long.

Though it’s difficult to chronicle any element of Smith’s life without injecting at least a hint of tabloid sensationalism, writer-director Thane Economou (“The Wedding Party”) takes an aggressively cheeky approach to the saga of Kapoor’s involvement, in the process undercutting what he clearly intends to be an empathetic portrait of both the doctor and his patient. Taking the lead in a rare film focused on a prominent Indian American, Kal Penn struggles to wrangle this flamboyant biopic into a serious acting challenge, but he delivers impressive work in its final scenes even if they fail to elevate what came before them.

Penn plays Kapoor, a closeted physician who takes over a retiring colleague’s practice, in the process inheriting Anna Nicole Smith ( Abbie Cornish ) as a patient. Like his predecessor, Sandeep agrees to treat Smith under a pseudonym, but she quickly beguiles him with her childlike charm; despite his attempts to maintain a professional distance, he soon becomes a part of her inner circle. Shortly after she invites him to ride in a Los Angeles Pride parade where he participates in a self-described “orgy,” Anna announces that she’s pregnant — with whose baby, he does not know. Even so, he determines that failing to prescribe methadone to curb her festering drug addiction could harm her pregnancy, so he reluctantly writes a big order for her to take with her on a weeks-long trip to the Bahamas.

Popular on Variety

She eventually gives birth to a daughter, Dannielynn, and just three days later, loses her son Daniel (Jordan Kronis) to an overdose. A few months later, Sandeep learns from news reports that Anna herself has overdosed; he rushes to his office to confiscate her and Daniel’s medical files to protect them from being stolen or leaked, but the media has already staked out his practice. At the urging of a devoted patient, Margie (Jocelyne Zucco), he retains no-nonsense attorney Ellen Garofalo (Linda Hamilton) and mounts a PR campaign to present himself as the upstanding medical professional he claims to be. But when federal investigators discover Anna’s medical records in his underwear drawer, he becomes an official suspect in her death.

Eventually, the attorney general working at the direction of gubernatorial hopeful Jerry Brown charges Sandeep, along with Smith’s lawyer Howard K. Stern (David Julian Hirsh) and her psychiatrist Khristine Eroshevich (Virginia Cowan), of criminal conspiracy, with him as the lead plaintiff. As he fights to clear his name, Sandeep unexpectedly discovers that his best ally to win the case may be Harvey Levin (Elon Gold), the TMZ journalist whose photos first incriminated him, even as he reckons with the cost of his relationship with Smith on his family, his practice and his future.

According to this film, Sandeep Kapoor was kind of a nitwit regarding his time in the spotlight, but he ultimately occupied only a marginal place in Anna Nicole Smith’s story. His famous patient passes away 25 minutes into the film; the remaining 86 minutes focus on Garofalo’s legal maneuverings and his own incredulity at virtually every part of the process of being put through the public wringer.

Given Smith’s celebrity status and the sensational ups and downs of her life, it’s easy for an audience unfamiliar with Kapoor’s memoir, which inspired the film, to assume that he was a sycophant and enabler of this troubled woman. Economou seems to want to do justice to both his and his patient’s lives, but his script obfuscates Kapoor’s involvement in her death more than necessary by jumping back and forth in time, peppering what was already intriguing subject matter with fourth-wall-breaking monologues, montages that meld real and staged footage and at least one sidebar about a character who, though objectively interesting, is more or less totally irrelevant to this story.

Events such as his interview with Levin — as Garofalo’s legal strategy or his personal leap into the belly of the media beast — are especially fascinating when we see actual footage of their conversation over the closing credits. But they are unfortunately sandwiched between reams of expository commentary about each participant’s real and imagined motivations, political undertones of the lawsuit brought against him, and Kapoor’s only semi-convincing protestations of his innocence.

Understandably, Penn struggles to hold these disparate points of focus together with a performance that vacillates between disarmingly dopey and almost willfully ignorant of the realities of the 2000s media landscape. It does not help that, outside of Hamilton as his tough-as-nails defense lawyer, the rest of the performances are delivered at an almost parodic pitch, led by Cornish with a rendition of Smith that seems pitched more to “Saturday Night Live” than a real film for the big screen.

All of which is to say “Trust Me, I’m A Doctor” probably would have worked better as a documentary than as a narrative feature. Even taking Kapoor at his word that he never wanted and was happy to recede afterward from the public eye, Economou clearly possesses an impressive enough archive of material to tell this story with or without his participation, with the same multimedia flair that he deploys here. If nothing else, moviegoers wouldn’t have had to watch Cornish play Smith, an admittedly unenviable acting tightrope that she navigates clumsily at best. Kapoor, meanwhile, seems much more self-possessed in the real footage, making him precisely as sympathetic as the filmmaker intended.

Following a handful of genuinely powerful scenes by Penn that sadly come too late to offset the circus-like tone established earlier, the film concludes with a montage detailing what happened to everyone involved after the verdict was handed down in Kapoor’s case. The overarching message of that sequence is that something about celebrity worship seems to drive people crazy, imagining anything connected to it as more significant than it actually is. With respect to Kapoor, Economou should have paid more attention to the epiphanies of his own film; the rollercoaster of Smith’s life will always be a curio, but that doesn’t mean that every passenger on it has a story worth telling.

article_text:
Filme tem direção de Nathan Fielder e Lance Oppenheim.

A 24 divulgou o primeiro teaser de “ You Can See Everything “, documentário de Nathan Fielder e Lance Oppenheim sobre Elizabeth Holmes. Assista acima (sem legendas).

Foi divulgado também o primeiro cartaz internacional do filme, abaixo.

Diz a sinopse:

“Trinta e quatro dias antes de ser enviada para a prisão, a notória fundadora do Vale do Silício, Elizabeth Holmes, convida uma equipe de filmagem cética para documentar cada um de seus passos. O que começa como um retrato íntimo de uma condenada enigmática transforma-se em uma jornada alucinante de três anos rumo ao abismo.”

Holmes ficou conhecida ao fundar a startup de biotecnologia Theranos e inventar um suposto dispositivo milagroso de triagem sanguínea, sendo condenada por fraude pouco depois. Trata-se de um dos casos mais emblemáticos da justiça estadunidense, sendo tema de diversos documentários, dramatizações e reportagens investigativas.

“You Can See Everything” tem direção de Nathan Fielder, conhecido pelas séries “Nathan For You” e “O Ensaio”, e Lance Oppenheim. A dupla produziu a obra em segredo ao longo dos últimos quatro anos, utilizando imagens de Holmes e de seu parceiro; o casal os convidou para morar em sua casa e registrar o cotidiano de ambos nos 34 dias que antecederam a prisão dela.

“You Can See Everything” estreia nos EUA em 16 de outubro, ainda sem data brasileira.

article_text:
Source: Universal

‘The Odyssey’

EXCLUSIVE: Universal Pictures International UK & Ireland has broken its annual box office record in 2026 with 10 weeks of the year still to go.

Films released by the studio have grossed a total of £284.9m, beating the £280.2m taken across 2015. They account for 28% of all UK-Ireland box office takings so far this year.

The studio has three of the top five films of the year: The Odyssey , Michael and The Super Mario Galaxy Movie. Additionally, Minions & Monsters is in the top 10.

Still playing in cinemas after 14 weekends, Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey is the second-highest-grossing film of the year with £87.8m, and is the 10 th -highest-grossing film of all time in the territory. It has taken a significant 31% – £27m – of its total to date from Imax screenings.

The studio has also become the first since the pandemic to have five films take over £20m in a single year, with Obsession crossing that mark last month. Curry Barker’s smash hit is the third-highest-grossing horror film of all time in the territory.

It is the fourth-highest total ever for a studio in the territory, with Disney holding the top three spots from 2019 (£489.7m), 2018 (£312.6m) and 2016 (£300.7m). If takings continue at the current rate, Universal will surpass the latter two and record the second-highest annual total ever by the end of the year.

“With 2026 marking Universal Pictures UK and Ireland’s best year ever at the box office, we’re incredibly proud of our filmmakers and partners, whose extraordinary range of films, from blockbusters and original filmmaking to animation, literary drama, horror and event cinema, has given audiences a different reason to visit the cinema,” said Kezia Williams, managing director of Universal Pictures International UK & Ireland. “And to have reached this milestone in October, with many of our films still in cinemas and five more to come before the end of the year, makes it even more special.”

Recent releases still in cinemas include literary adaptation Sense And Sensibility , horror Other Mommy and animation Forgotten Island ; while the upcoming slate consists of I Love Boosters (October 30), George Michael – The Faith Tour (November 6), A Talent For Murder (November 20), Violent Night 2 (December 4) and Onslaught (December 11).

“It’s an incredibly positive sign for cinemagoing more broadly that there is no better place to be entertained, moved, surprised or transported by films than on the big screen, it is a reminder of why films and cinemas continue to matter so much to our culture,” added Williams.

article_text:
That this Autumn’s riots in France have occurred – and that the artworld, ever keen to wash its hands of politics when unable to dictate them, ran scared – can be seen as nothing else but inevitable

‘I was scared to come so I’m here,’ read one of the placards held up by a teenager at the protest that brought hundreds of thousands of people onto the streets of Paris last Saturday. On another was a photomontage of French President Emmanuel Macron, smirking, with the Champs-Élysées on fire behind him.

Also scared were the dons and doyennes of the Art Basel Paris art fair, a shopping mall for the world’s visiting elite, which opted to close before the protests for the ‘safety of everyone involved’. Because, in the space of a few weeks, what began as a high-school-student movement demanding better learning conditions has escalated into nationwide civil unrest, reaching a violent head on 17 October. The students’ concerns were pretty reasonable: deteriorating school conditions, a shortage of teachers and the pressures of Parcoursup, France’s algorithm-based university admissions platform.

As the government continued to ignore them, long refusing to meet with student representatives, the movement grew wider and angrier, eventually becoming a much broader expression of dissent over the rising cost of living, deteriorating public services and a president who is behaving increasingly like a monarch ( Sus au roi! – down with the king – was a recurring protest slogan of these marches). Teachers, health workers, firefighters and former gilets jaunes joined the mobilisation; university students set up blockades and occupied campuses. Taken together, their grievances paint a pretty bleak picture of France after almost ten years under Macron: public services starved of resources, further cuts to education and culture, and environmental policies that continue to favour short-term economic interests over ecological concerns. Meanwhile, the president’s government has slowly but surely brought far-right ideas into the political mainstream, normalising anti-immigration and hardline security rhetoric, and bringing its proponents closer to power. The next presidential election is just six months away.

No longer able to ignore the movement, the government reached for a familiar solution: violent police repression. On 24 October, 70,000 police officers and gendarmes were deployed nationwide, backed by specialist tactical units and armoured vehicles, who unleashed water cannons, teargas, stun grenades and rubber bullets on the public. Their violence has left dozens of teenagers with life-changing injuries: a fifteen-year-old in Lens lost a hand after being struck by a stun grenade; another teenager had his jaw shattered after being hit at close range by a grenade launcher. Yet the president, his interior minister and large portions of the media have gone to almost absurd lengths to highlight the tragedy of the damage inflicted by the casseurs , or rioters. The leftosphere responded online, offering its deepest condolences to the families of the dustbins burnt on 17 October.

What received rather less attention were the claims at the heart of the protests, or the social conditions that brought France to this point. Both in 2023 and 2024, 9.8 million people in metropolitan France were living below the poverty line – 15.4 percent of the population, the highest rate since the country’s Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies began measuring in 1996 – while income inequality reached a record high. Rather than addressing these underlying conditions, increasingly influential rightwing media voices have coopted the protests to fuel anti-immigration and Islamophobic discourse. On TV, far-right politician Éric Zemmour described the looters as “hordes of Maghrebi and African barbarians entering the cities”. On 23 October a gunman armed with a submachine gun opened fire from his car window in Trappes, a banlieue southwest of Paris, killing French MMA fighter Pengo Bossio Wangi and wounding five others. He reportedly told investigators that he wanted to avenge shopkeepers targeted during the looting on 17 October, and had deliberately set out to shoot Black people and Arabs.

As one of the hundreds of thousands of protesters who have marched in Paris and Toulouse – where I live – since the movement began, I have mostly seen peaceful crowds dancing, accompanied by brass bands and carrying placards that are both hilarious and brutally lucid. And , perhaps more surprisingly, teenagers waving French flags and bursting into ‘La Marseillaise’. What I have also witnessed, as I have over the past ten years of protesting, is the overwhelming and disproportionate use of force: crowds of unarmed citizens kettled – surrounded by police and prevented from moving freely – before being charged and teargassed; police searches at the start of marches, with protective equipment including swimming goggles, masks and saline solution used to mitigate the effects of teargas confiscated; and racial slurs directed at protesters by officers. And then there is the staggering number of arrests: 8,000 in a single month – a figure that anthropologist Chowra Makaremi pointed out in a recent interview with Equator was ‘surpassed only by events like 17 October 1961, when police detained over 12,000 Algerians in Paris, killing hundreds and throwing their bodies into the Seine’.

At the heart of the storm, rampant wealth. Art Basel Paris in the Grand Palais proceeded almost as usual – until it didn’t. The fair recorded millions in sales in its first days, as collectors came and went while the protests raged outside. Within the fair, the unrest was largely discussed in the same terms as the government’s response: as a problem of public order. On 22 October the fair announced that it would close two days early, citing the need to protect visitors, exhibitors, staff and artworks from demonstrations planned for the weekend. One post, widely shared on Instagram, targeted the fair itself: the collective Pillage de Classe called for the ‘reclaiming’ of the Grand Palais, denouncing Art Basel Paris as a ‘plundering fair’ that allows the superrich to shield their wealth from tax.

That a commercial machine like Art Basel should remain largely indifferent to the social realities of the city it descends upon for a week each year comes as no surprise. The artworld has long been good at turning rebellion into a selling point, celebrating radical ideas while happily profiting from the very inequalities they seek to challenge (‘The artworld loves rebellion provided it’s framed, insured and hanging in a gallery’, goes a meme ). The protests brought into sharp relief the inequalities that Art Basel can usually afford to keep at a distance. The fair didn’t cause this unrest, of course, but its presence in Paris became a striking symbol of the concentration of wealth and power against which so many are protesting. Where’s all the money gone? Well, here’s one hiding place.

As I write, the protests continue, and I doubt the movement will subside so easily, intimidation notwithstanding. I may be scared to go out and protest, too, but I’m galvanised by a generation refusing to have its future decided for it. The presidential election is six months away; the fight over what comes next has barely begun. Standing on top of a bus stop, a kid held up a sign that read ‘ Gen-Z vaincra ’. Gen Z will prevail. A bold claim, perhaps, but one worth fighting for.

article_text:
At the Katonah Museum of Art in New York, ‘Intermittent Islands: Four Caribbean Women Artists’ brings together Belkis Ayón, Yanira Collado, Marielle Plaisir and Lisa C Soto to explore diaspora, cultural memory and the complexities of Caribbean identity.

How do histories of displacement shape our understanding of home? In ‘Intermittent Islands: Four Caribbean Women Artists’, four artists examine the Caribbean as a space of cultural exchange, historical rupture and continuing transformation.

Bringing together the practices of Belkis Ayón, Yanira Collado, Marielle Plaisir and Lisa C Soto, the exhibition explores how personal experience and collective history intersect across generations and geographies.

Cuban printmaker Ayón draws on Afro-Cuban spiritual traditions, using monumental collographs to investigate mythology and cultural identity. Collado employs textiles, construction materials and found objects to explore memory, labour and the transmission of cultural knowledge.

Plaisir examines histories of race, power and social inequality through figurative works that challenge inherited narratives. At the same time, Soto combines natural and industrial materials to question relationships between territory, identity and belonging.

Working across printmaking, collage, textiles and installation, the artists reveal how material practices can preserve histories while generating new understandings of identity.

Rather than presenting the Caribbean as a singular geographical or cultural identity, Intermittent Islands foregrounds its interconnected histories and diasporic experiences, inviting audiences to reconsider how memory, migration and artistic expression shape our relationships with place.

This exhibition is on view at the Katonah Museum of Art in New York until 24 January 2027.

In hoeverre bestaat het leven uit het reproduceren van rollen en rolpatronen die door de maatschappij zijn opgelegd? Wie bepaalt welke rollen er zijn? Wat is de werking van macht? Hoe kan ze beteugeld worden? Deze veelomvattende, urgente vragen legt Kamau Ng’ang’a aan zijn publiek voor in Kunstenlab te Deventer met zijn tentoonstelling You’re a Lucky Fellow Mr. Smith. In dit essay reflecteert Linde Keja op de antropologische reikwijdte van dit werk.

In Kunstenlab is een houten installatie gebouwd die de grote zaal vult. Een open structuur die bestaat uit een eetkamer, woonkamer en slaapkamer. In elke kamer staan drie surround-soundsystemen en diverse HiFi-installaties waaruit geluidsfragmenten klinken.

De bewoners van het huis, Mr. en Mrs. Smith zijn twee poppen van ruim twee meter hoog, gemaakt van stukken resthout en uitstekende spijkers. Naast het huis staat een bank, waar het echtpaar af en toe buiten zit. De audiofragmenten zijn afkomstig uit de United States National Archives en bestaan onder andere uit delen van speeches van voormalig president Nixon en uit telefoongesprekken die hij voerde met Henry Kissinger en H.R. ‘Bob’ Haldeman. De audio is vrijgegeven naar aanleiding van onderzoek ten tijde van het Watergate schandaal in de jaren ‘70 van de vorige eeuw. De kakafonie van geluid vorm de achtergrond van de levens van Mr. en Mrs. Smith.

De titel van het werk, You’re a Lucky Fellow Mr. Smith , heeft Kamau Ng’ang’a ontleend aan een komische musicalfilm uit 1943, over een romance van een jonge vrouw en een soldaat. Later is een lied met eenzelfde titel uitgebracht door Frank Sinatra. Uit het laatste couplet: ‘You should thank your lucky stars and I mean, there are 50 in your flag.[…], your speech is free, [..], You should look at the great constitution that we got. […] I don’t care if you haven’t a cent. You can still have things your own way, on each election day. […] You’re a fortunate fellow, (yes, a fortunate fellow), And a privileged person (and a privileged person), You’re a lucky fellow, Mr. Smith’.

De kunstenaar, geboren in Zuid-Afrika, studeerde twee jaren geleden af aan de Koninklijke Academie van Beeldende Kunsten in Den Haag. In zijn eerdere installaties, Getting comfortable in your skinsuit (2023) en People Watching (2024), speelden ook grote houten figuren een rol in huiselijke scènes, waarin videowerk werd getoond. De video’s zijn montages van bewegende archiefbeelden en -geluiden, waarvan de originelen gemaakt zijn door, of in opdracht van de Amerikaanse overheid tussen de jaren ‘30 en ‘70 van de vorige eeuw. De werken van Ng’ang’a komen voort uit zijn omvangrijke onderzoek van de afgelopen acht jaar, in online archieven als de United States National Archives . In het werk Getting comfortable in your skinsuit (2023) zit een scène waarin de houten figuren als een familie bij elkaar zitten in een woonkamer en televisiekijken. De televisie toont een videowerk dat de kijker informeert over hoe je een beter persoon kan worden voor jezelf en je omgeving. Het concept van ‘zelf’ wordt benoemd als iets dat te creëren is en waaraan je kan werken: ‘.. men and women of tomorrow..get the most out of life.. . we are what we believe … you have a choice.. by a better understanding of patterns of everyday life and by knowing how you respond to various stimuli you can balance your emotions and use them so that your personality becomes more pleasant’.

Het zijn veelomvattende, urgente vragen die Ng’ang’a onderzoekt en voorlegt aan het publiek. Een vraag die een centrale plaats inneemt, is de manier waarop de staat invloed heeft op het leven van individuen. In de zaalfilm vertelt de kunstenaar over het zichtbaar maken van soft coersion /zachte dwang, die via media de huiselijke sfeer binnenkomt. De media oefenen volgens hem een vorm van soft power uit door het produceren van narratieven met algemeen geaccepteerde ideeën over hoe we leven en wie we zijn. Een vorm van beïnvloeding, waardoor ons gedrag universeel wordt en het algemeen geaccepteerde ideaalbeeld wordt versterkt.

In hoeverre bestaat het leven uit het reproduceren van rollen en rolpatronen die door de maatschappij zijn opgelegd? Wie bepaalt welke rollen er zijn? Wat is de werking van macht? Hoe kan ze beteugeld worden?

[i] De cultuur waarin je opgroeit, vormt een normatief kader, waarin processen van in- en uitsluiting spelen. Wanneer hoort iemand erbij en wanneer is iemand ‘anders’? In politieke vraagstukken zijn naast opvattingen, feiten en onderzoek naar feiten van belang. Omdat mensen geneigd zijn hiërarchieën te vormen, neemt de macht van sommigen toe ten opzichte van anderen. Er worden allianties gevormd, samenwerkingen. In hoeverre mensen in staat zijn zich in posities van macht te manoeuvreren, hangt af van zowel persoonlijke, sociale, economische, politieke en historische factoren. [ii]

Ozymandias is een vergriekste benaming van Ramses II, die beschouwd wordt als een van de grote farao’s uit het oude Egypte. Dit speelt sinds het begin van de westerse wetenschap in de 16 e eeuw, na de zogenoemde ontdekkingsreizen in de 15 e eeuw tot op heden.

Met vormen van staatsinrichtingen wordt geprobeerd om de macht te beteugelen, zoals in democratie met de scheiding van de wetgevende, uitvoerende en rechterlijke macht. Het behoeft geen uitleg dat dit geen garantie is voor een beleid waarin het algemeen belang leidend is. Of een garantie zou zijn dat een staat zijn geweldsmonopolie gebruikt op legitieme gronden. [4] Het zogenoemde nationale belang en de nationale veiligheid worden, als een soort uitvergroot eigenbelang, gebruikt als reden om geweld te gebruiken tegen ‘anderen’, naties of bevolkingsgroepen. Macht hanteren vraagt op persoonlijk niveau om karakter. In het werk Disease of Character (2022), een 3D model van een heerser, is een personage te zien op een grote stoel op een verhoging met een lange, goudkleurige staf in zijn hand. Achter de stoel bevindt zich een roodoranje stralenkrans, als een zon die de belichaming van de macht verlicht. Bij beter kijken is te zien dat het gezicht vanaf de bovenkaak is aangevreten en in ontbinding is.

In een tijd die ook wel als post-truth wordt aangeduid, is zelfbewustzijn geen luxe. Een individu wordt actor wanneer degene zich bewust is van zijn potentie tot handelen. In het videowerk in de installatie People Watching (2024) worden mensen gefilmd, terwijl ze zich bewust worden van het feit dat ze worden gefilmd. Wanneer ze zich dit realiseren, worden ze zichtbaar ongemakkelijk en veranderen hun gedrag. Dit is het moment waarop ze een rol aannemen, performers worden, zoals acteurs voor een publiek.

Identificatie met een rol is voor een deel noodzaak om te functioneren in het sociale verkeer. De kwetsbaarheid zit vooral in de verwarring van de rol en het zelf. In het uitoefenen van macht, wordt de macht meer legitiem wanneer zij onpersoonlijk wordt gemaakt, niet gedreven door eigenbelang. Depersonalisatie en officialiteit gaan samen en impliceren een zeker verlies dat geldt voor ieder lid van de samenleving, namelijk de relativering van het zelf als middelpunt van de wereld. [5] De reeks werken Premonition (2022) van Ng’ang’a, acht hoofden gemaakt van gips, raakt aan dit onderwerp. De sculpturen zijn beschadigd door de impact van een hard voorwerp. ‘Through this series I explored a more methaphorical obsession with the conceptual destruction of the self as a true and believed entity through the physical destruction of my likeness through an intensely-physical, labour intensive process’ , aldus de omschrijving van de kunstenaar.

In de tentoonstelling bij Kunstenlab houdt Ng’ang’a verschillende keren een performance in de installatie die hij bouwde. Het publiek krijgt een kijk in het dagelijkse leven van Mr. en Mrs. Smith. Hun conversaties bestaan uit bewerkte audiofragmenten uit Amerikaanse romantische films uit de jaren ‘30 van de vorige eeuw: ‘..Do you really love me? Yes, I do..’ . De performance bestaat uit vier akten, waarbij de poppen zich steeds op een andere plaats in het huis bevinden. Voor deze installatie maakte de kunstenaar de houten figuren voor het eerst flexibel en treedt hij op als aanwezige poppenspeler. We zien Ng’ang’a, gekleed in driedelig pak, de houten figuren optillen en verplaatsen, ze zijn groter dan hij en tamelijk zwaar. De kunstenaar is voortdurend bezig de poppen in de juiste houdingen te krijgen. Als één van de poppen opzij zakt, zet Ng’ang’a hem recht en legt de arm van de ene om de schouder van de andere pop. In wankele evenwichten worden de poppen tot leven gewekt. Er lijkt een nieuwe relatie te ontstaan tussen poppen en poppenspeler, waarbij onhandigheid, ongemak, afhankelijkheid en zorg van de kunstenaar voor zijn creaties zichtbaar worden. Mr. en Mrs. Smith laten het zich graag aanleunen. Wanneer het echtpaar op het punt staat om een wandeling te maken, gaat het regenen en besluiten ze om toch binnen te blijven. Ze hullen zich liever in de warmte van het huis en de narratieven die ze doen geloven dat ze zo’n goed leven hebben in zo’n geweldig land.

De tentoonstelling You’re a Lucky Fellow Mr. Smith is te zien t/m 4 januari 2027.

article_text:
Films and events

Journey

The Secret Lives of Baba Segi’s Wives

Daniel Oriahi’s wonderful adaptation of Lola Shoneyin’s acclaimed novel is an engrossing exploration of a highly traditional Yoruba household forced to confront hidden truths from its past.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director Daniel Oriahi

Screenwriters Adze Ugah, Daniel Oriahi, Heidi Uys, Mo Abudu

With Omowunmi Dada, Iyabo Ojo, Mercy Aigbe, Bimbo Ademoye

Nigeria 2026. 119min

Courtesy of The Baba Segi Collective

Languages Yoruba, English With some English subtitles

Introduction

In this gripping exploration of sexual politics, power and survival in present-day Nigeria, patriarch Baba Segi oversees a household with his three wives, a seemingly harmonious polyamorous arrangement with their children. However, with the arrival of his youngest university educated fourth wife and the revelation that she is unable to conceive, cracks begin to appear in the facade, undermining the dynamics of Segi’s world. Oriahi foregrounds the women’s lives and stories in this compelling film.

Isabel Moir

Content advice

Contains scenes of sex and sexual violence.

Contains themes of abortion.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

Ben’Imana

This Cannes Camera d’Or winner unfolds in the shadow of the 1994 Rwandan genocide, exploring its legacy and the possibility of forgiveness.

Clarissa

Sophie Okonedo shines in Arie and Chuko Esiri’s (Eyimofe, LFF 2020) sophomore feature film, a delicate, sun-soaked re-imagining of Mrs Dalloway, set in contemporary Lagos.

Once Upon a Time in Harlem

Filmed by William Greaves in 1972 and completed by his son David 50 years later, this is a rapturous love letter to the Harlem Renaissance.

article_text:
I Ninos Du Brasil rimangono un caso preziosamente irriverente per il panorama internazionale sia musicale che performativo. Sono Nico Vascellari e Nicolò Fortuni a formare storicamente il duo cult, col fine di coinvolgere il pubblico in un nuovo rito collettivo cui sentirsi atavicamente parte. Seguendo uno stile istintuale e sacrale, il loro repertorio spazia dalla batucada alla techno primordiale, dalla samba destrutturata alle percussioni ricavate da oggetti quotidiani. Un linguaggio fatto di suoni e gesti apparentemente casuali che, durante i live, ha portato a danzare fino a 30mila persone.

Dopo Vida Eterna e Antro Pop , esce il loro quinto album, Ordem Micelial , prodotto da Rocco Rampino , ora in tour tra Roma, Bari, Milano e Pordenone. Un disco che celebra l’underground ponendo al centro un organismo vivo e misterioso per spiegare l’espansione di una ricerca che affonda le radici nel post-punk fino a «Un’esplosione di rock crudo e garage che ricorda lo spirito psichedelico e dance dei Primal Scream ».

Il tema estetico dell’album ruota attorno all’immagine e alla biologia del micelio, la rete sotterranea dei funghi cui gli autori dedicano la copertina, partecipando col proprio corpo alla mimesi. Il fungo emerge dal terreno senza svelarsi per intero, lasciando invisibile ciò che rimane collegato. Si tratta di una metafora di trasformazione e sopravvivenza che incontriamo già nella produzione di Vascellari, a partire dalle sue riviste Vogue sepolte, esposte nel 2023 a Forte Belvedere a Firenze . Tali opere, ricoperte da muschi e licheni dopo il gesto di “seppellirle”, implicano un tentativo di decomposizione che guarda al black-metal norvegese, secondo una «Non differenziazione che permette di scavare in noi qualcosa che è stato dimenticato, ma non distrutto».

Questo passaggio è documentato dal video ufficiale di Carlos Casas , tra materiale d’archivio e telecamere endoscopiche che riprendono da vicino le reti nascoste di una natura incontaminata. Le immagini si dissolvono e si amalgamano rapidamente, simili a spore e come i ritmi dei Ninos Du Brasil, che ci rigenerano in forme sempre nuove e inaspettate, oltre la superficie.

article_text:
Encore récemment, Elizabeth Holmes était « juste » une femme d’affaires condamnée pour escroquerie, largement inconnue du public français. Aux États-Unis, son entreprise Theranos et la machine d’analyse sanguine frauduleuse qu’elle a mise au point ont fait d’elle une paria, particulièrement détestée depuis son procès et la sortie de The Dropout , une série qui lui est dédiée et où elle apparaît sous les traits d’Amanda Seyfried.

Mais depuis septembre dernier, toutes les certitudes de millions de spectateur·ices volent en éclats (les séances affichent complet partout, le film a déjà rapporté plus de 45 millions de dollars et s’impose comme l’un des documentaires les plus rentables de l’histoire). Nathan Fielder, maître du high concept et de la cringe comedy , dévoile trois heures de documentaire filmées durant les trente jours précédant son incarcération en 2023.

Jusque dans sa manière de filmer en très gros plans, il essaie de comprendre ce qui se passe derrière ces gros yeux bleus. Elizabeth Holmes est-elle en train de le séduire et de l’arnaquer lui aussi en le persuadant qu’elle est innocente, ou est-elle en plein déni ? Est-elle totalement irresponsable, ou alors neuroatypique (elle dit n’avoir jamais menti de sa vie, ne saisit pas une situation comique basée sur un jeu de mots, etc.) ?

Sans dévoiler les tenants et aboutissants de la rupture formelle et méta qu’offre la deuxième partie du film, le film se poursuit après son incarcération. En l’absence de réponses convaincantes aux premières questions posées, Fielder, qui est présent à l’écran, continue d’enquêter auprès du mari d’Elizabeth Holmes et par des appels téléphoniques à la prison où elle est incarcérée.

Le film s’épaissit alors de plusieurs nouvelles couches documentaires, qui placent Fielder à équidistance de la fiction et du documentaire, et pointent l’incapacité des deux formes à approcher la vérité de cette femme. De nombreuses questions restent d’ailleurs sans réponses, dont certaines très inconfortables quant à la non-assistance de l’équipe du film face à une femme potentiellement sous emprise (à moins qu’il ne s’agisse encore de manipulation ?).

Expérience déroutante, You Can See Everything perturbe même après sa fin, puisque le cas Holmes semble loin d’être conclu (Fielder continuerait de recevoir des appels). Et la réalité des faits reste loin d’être cernée.

You Can See Everything , sortie le 30 décembre

article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "N ine years after superhero epic Justice League arrived in cinemas, there ought to be very little left to say about how it all went wrong. Zack Snyder shot the film, Joss Whedon substantially rewrote and reshot it, and audiences eventually got to see both men’s versions. Any debate over their relative merits long ago disappeared. Whedon is pretty much cancelled; Snyder has reinvented himself as the writer-director of extremely average ersatz Star Wars movies for Netflix, and an entirely new DC universe is under way that has very little to do with either of them.", "links": [{"text": "Joss Whedon", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/culture/joss-whedon"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "To a greater or lesser extent, the world has moved on. But Ben Affleck’s latest comments raise an uncomfortable question about whether Snyder’s departure was ever presented honestly.
