article_text:
N ine years after superhero epic Justice League arrived in cinemas, there ought to be very little left to say about how it all went wrong. Zack Snyder shot the film, Joss Whedon substantially rewrote and reshot it, and audiences eventually got to see both men’s versions. Any debate over their relative merits long ago disappeared. Whedon is pretty much cancelled; Snyder has reinvented himself as the writer-director of extremely average ersatz Star Wars movies for Netflix, and an entirely new DC universe is under way that has very little to do with either of them.

To a greater or lesser extent, the world has moved on. But Ben Affleck’s latest comments raise an uncomfortable question about whether Snyder’s departure was ever presented honestly. Speaking to Josh Horowitz on the Happy Sad Confused podcast , Affleck, who played Batman, described the Justice League reshoots as the lowest point of his career, but reserved his strongest criticism for the circumstances of Snyder’s departure. The director stepped away in May 2017 , two months after his daughter Autumn killed herself, aged 20, with the public explanation that he needed to be with his family. Affleck, however, alleged that studio Warner Bros had used the tragedy to justify replacing him. “The way in which that was, I thought, used as an excuse was one of the shittiest things I’ve ever seen,” Affleck said. “It was so gross.”

In July 2020 another Justice League actor, Ray Fisher (who played Cyborg), accused Whedon of abusive and unprofessional behaviour , prompting WarnerMedia to launch an investigation into the film’s production. In December 2020, the company announced the probe had concluded and said that unspecified “remedial action” had been taken . In May 2021, Gal Gadot (who played Wonder Woman) said Whedon had “threatened her career” during production of the film. Whedon denied both allegations in January 2022 , but has been largely absent from Hollywood since.

Affleck stressed that much of what he knew about his co-stars’ experiences came secondhand. His reaction was blunt: “Wow. This is about as gross as it gets.” On Snyder eventually releasing his own version ( a four-hour-plus extended take that became a draw for Warner’s fledgling HBO Max streaming platform after a fierce social media campaign by Snyder fans), he added: “That was fucking great. I was really happy for him.”

This is a story that seems to shift and morph the more time passes. Initially, the baton being passed from Snyder to Whedon was framed as a mercy, though there were rumours as early as February 2018 that Snyder might have been forced out for creative reasons . Now, almost a decade on, the film’s biggest star feels comfortable alleging that Warners used a family death to justify bringing in Whedon, who at the time was one of the biggest names in superhero movies (having overseen Marvel’s early Avengers films), but whose breezy, wisecracking writing style couldn’t have been further from Snyder’s furrow-browed, heavy-metal film-making. Warners had spent years allowing Snyder to turn its superheroes into tormented deities, then developed an urgent concern that none of them knew how to do banter.

If what actually happened matters, in 2026, it’s because this was the moment that the DC extended universe (DCEU) really began to enter its death spiral. Snyder had probably already lost the confidence of studio executives after 2016’s Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice tanked with critics, but audiences had still flocked to see that movie to the tune of $874m at the global box office . If a Snyder-led Justice League had reached cinemas in 2017 and proved a hit, it’s not impossible to imagine Warners allowing him to continue his vision for the future of the comic book studio. While the director of Watchmen wasn’t exactly the Kevin Feige of DC, he controlled the general direction of travel as the guy who oversaw its highest-profile ensemble efforts. After Justice League, the DCEU’s films crossed $500m at the worldwide box office only once, with 2018’s Aquaman. Somewhere along the way, the promise that everything was connected had become a warning that you might need to slog through another one.

The decline, to be fair, cannot all be blamed on one disastrous handover: the pandemic alone was probably responsible for at least some of the dramatic downturn in the DCEU’s fortunes after 2018. Nor does it follow that Snyder would have necessarily delivered a triumphant decade of superbly interconnected superhero cinema if everyone had simply left him to get on with it. His films could be ponderous, self-important and oddly embarrassed by the possibility that being Superman might occasionally be enjoyable. I’m not sure I even want to visit the alternative universe in which this grand plan actually came to fruition but it seems like a lot of DC fans at the time did.

Instead, Batman and Superman discovered themselves trapped in a universe whose supreme beings could create entire galaxies but found it impossible to agree on the appropriate number of jokes. Affleck’s comments bring us back to the human cost of all that studio indecision. Nine years on, DC has built a new universe, but still struggles to explain what happened to the old one.

article_text:
‘E armuffs!” says Sam Rockwell, pausing his gushing tribute mid-flow and turning to face John Malkovich on the couch. Rockwell loves Malkovich and has been discussing his work at some length. Malkovich, he says, is charismatic and dangerous, half masculine, half feminine; a unique combination and the perfect sparring partner. He’s one of the world’s finest actors and annoyingly modest to boot. “Earmuffs!” says Rockwell and pivots back towards me. “He hates hearing all this. That’s why I keep saying ‘earmuffs’.”

Malkovich frowns. “I don’t mind it,” he says.

“Hates it,” says Rockwell. “He truly hates all this stuff.”

In Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine , Malkovich and Rockwell play bickering CIA agents who may also be the best of friends. Chris and Lee are fresh from plotting the 1973 coup in Chile and are spinning their wheels on Rapa Nui, amid the crashing waves and the moai statues. They’ve seen too much and sinned too greatly and now Chris has cancer, which is hardly helping his mood. So he takes Lee aside and asks for one last big favour.

Ahead of the film’s premiere, the production team commandeer suites at an opulent Venice hotel and hand out hats and T-shirts to each new arrival. The lobby becomes a sea of merch. The harried concierge has to raise his voice to be heard. He says: “Second floor for the Six White Horses press interviews.”

McDonagh makes films that are playful and volatile, spring-loaded with violence and spiced with absurdist black comedy. Wild Horse Nine nods to In Bruges and The Banshees of Inisherin with its odd-couple antics and explosive side notes. But its mood is more mournful, death-haunted, with one eye on the past. McDonagh – once the upstart enfant terrible of London theatre – is now a silver-haired 56-year-old who comes at life from a different angle. “I’m getting older,” he says. “Maybe this is my first old-man movie.”

On sitting down to script Wild Horse Nine, the film-maker wrote GUILT and REGRET at the top of page one, as though setting his course with a compass and sextant. His film opens in Santiago before relocating to the South Pacific. From there it homes in on Malkovich’s CIA veteran, a leaky repository of cold war horror with his memories of the Bay of Pigs and Dealey Plaza. Chris is likely dying and wants to go out with a bang. He claims that he knows who killed JFK and is about to spill the beans.

The Kennedy assassination is the God particle of conspiracy theories. It marked the loss of US innocence, or the start of the rot of disinformation and fake news. McDonagh knows the official version and remains breezily unconvinced. “I definitely think there was something going on,” he says. “I’m definitely a believer in the conspiracy. Exactly what that was, we’ll never really know. Was Lee Harvey Oswald involved? More than likely. Was he the lone gunman? I don’t believe that for a second.”

He’s made several pictures with Woody Harrelson. Wasn’t Harrelson’s father once rumoured to have been involved in the killing? McDonagh sits up and mimes zipping his lip. “I know nothing,” he says.

Wild Horse Nine was never intended as a comment on the present-day United States. Except that history has a tendency to repeat and the shoot coincided with Donald Trump’s strike on Venezuela. Operations like that used to be more covert, conducted via proxies, whereas now they seem brazen, the equivalent of a smash-and-grab raid. “But I don’t think Trump is the worst president that we’ve had,” he says. “I don’t even think he’s the worst in the past 60-years. Nixon was more of a fascist pig. George W Bush probably killed more people than Trump. And then if you look at Vietnam, there’s Johnson. The difference is that with old-timey fascism, you at least had to keep it secret. These days you don’t have to hide it any more. Is that more fucked? Or is it more honest?”

McDonagh sits behind one closed door; Rockwell and Malkovich behind another. On-screen or off, the two actors have different energies, different speeds, so that the interview feels like a private performance: the Energizer Bunny versus the all-seeing Sphinx. One of these men has left his sunglasses on the floor. Inevitably it is Rockwell, who is altogether more bouncy and heedless. “My Guccis,” he cries. “Oh man, I would have stepped on those.”

Rockwell won an Oscar for playing the bumptious small-town deputy in McDonagh’s Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri . Malkovich may well follow suit thanks to Wild Horse Nine, which goes on to receive a rapturous 13-minute ovation at the premiere. The 72-year-old is on fabulously flavourful form as Chris, a tragicomic monster who is simultaneously melting down and seeing the light, lashing out and making amends. The character plays to the actor’s natural strengths, mining his innate theatricality and enigmatic air. But he explains that the role required some heavy lifting as well. Endless rehearsals and hours of line-readings, he says. “Sam and I did each scene at least a thousand times.”

A thousand? Malkovich is so self-contained and unblinking, it’s hard to know when he’s joking.

Rockwell chips in. “Yeah, about a thousand times. We ran it on the weekends. John’s a workhorse.”

“You are, too,” Malkovich says. It’s good to have a co-star to rehearse with, he adds, although every good actor has their own way of working. Clint Eastwood, for instance, prefers to hit the ground running. “You have to be a slick talker to get more than two takes out of Clint. You have to be pretty convincing, because he doesn’t take that lightly. As I know from experience.”

They were on Rapa Nui for six weeks, which helped with the process. “I have two granddaughters, so it was a long time away from them,” he says. “I don’t like being away from my grandchildren. But it’s a great place to shoot because there’s nothing else to do. You can swim with the turtles but that’s about it. Your work days are long. You’re always prepping for tomorrow. If it weren’t for a movie, I’d probably go nuts.”

Rockwell enjoyed it. “We had a great time,” he says. “Every night we had a little Chile wine and some rum. And there was a drink made with sugarcane, what the hell was it called? They put an egg-white in it.”

His partner, the actor Leslie Bibb, has materialised in the doorway. “Pisco sour,” she says.

“Pisco sour!” He’s delighted to see her and glad of the intel. Bibb has swung by to check when Rockwell breaks for lunch. He introduces her to me and indicates Malkovich on the couch. “But you can’t miss John,” he says. “Look at him, he’s beautiful.”

Marooned on his island, Chris plans to write his memoirs and come clean. His bosses are terrified he’ll mention “the Dallas parts” of his story. Some secrets, they feel, must be taken to the grave.

Malkovich has played heroes and villains. He’s been Tom Ripley, Biff Loman and the Vicomte de Valmont. But his career has been long and he’s covered this particular topic before. In 1994, he adapted and directed a stage version of Libra, Don DeLillo’s novel about Lee Harvey Oswald. He studied the Zapruder footage of JFK’s final moments and wandered down several conspiracy rabbit holes. The Warren Commission’s findings, he concluded, were either flawed or a lie. And if that makes him a crank, he’s hardly in the minority.

“Well, I think 60% of the American public don’t believe it,” he says. “Could the official story be true? Yeah, I guess. So could Keebler elves. The government tells us all kinds of things. Some of them may be true but not the majority of them, that’s my experience.”

I’ve read that he hasn’t voted since the 1972 presidential election, when the liberal George McGovern lost in a landslide to Nixon. He nods; this is true. “I’m not a believer,” he says.

Not a believer in what? Democracy? Malkovich shrugs. “In the whole thing, really. As they say in France: ‘Je ne pratique pas’, I’m not practising. I remember the night McGovern lost. I was talking to my father on the phone and I said: ‘Well, I’m done.’ He said: ‘My God, John, you can’t be done.’ I was 19 years old but that was it, I was done. I concentrate on what I can make and leave it at that.”

What about Rockwell? Is he still practising? “Yeah, well, I vote,” he says glumly. “I vote with faint hope. Hoping Obama will come back.”

The publicist sticks her head around the door. She reports that lunch is almost ready, which means that we’ve reached the last question. Rockwell perks up. “No pressure,” he says.

Let’s finish with death. That’s where the whole film is leading. Chris has decided he wants to die on Rapa Nui. Then he changes his mind and opts for Venice instead. Assuming that a death can be scripted like a film, where in the world would be the ideal place to bow out?

Malkovich thinks for a moment. “Probably on stage,” he says. “About 15 years ago I toured with a new opera based on Casanova’s memoirs. It started with Casanova chasing a chambermaid around the stage, as he was known to do, and then he has a heart attack. The play stops and people come out with a stretcher and then everyone breaks into song. Before the performance, I always made sure to tell all my friends: ‘It’s just the beginning of the play. I fake a heart attack. Don’t pay any attention.’ But forgot to tell my then-agent and I don’t think she has ever forgiven me.”

A few nights after that, he made the exact same mistake. “I have a friend, Barbara Sturm, who is a knee doctor in Düsseldorf. She came to see me and I suddenly realised I hadn’t warned her either. So I tried to text from the dressing room but of course she already had her phone switched off, being a well-mannered person. And so blah-blah-blah, the whole thing happened again.”

The production was pure chaos, but it was also rather funny. Every night he’d fake a coronary and see the panic sweep through the audience like wildfire. “As many as 20 people would run up to the stage. You’d have the doctors and a stretcher and then everybody starts singing.”

Rockwell is laughing. “That’s good acting,” he says.

“Well no, it’s terrible,” says Malkovich. “But still, it wouldn’t be the worst way to go.”

article_text:
Yesterday, visitors to the fifth edition of Art Basel Paris had the chance to preview its “Hors les murs” program, which spreads monumental artworks across nine exceptional cultural and heritage sites in the French capital. Among the highlights are works by Niki de Saint Phalle and Alicja Kwade, displayed along Avenue Winston Churchill, between the Grand Palais and the Petit Palais.

Yet these encounters also serve as reminders of what the program has lost. Kwade and Saint Phalle were previously featured on Place Vendôme and in the Tuileries, respectively, but both of those venues are now absent from the itinerary, as are the Institut de France, the Musée Eugène-Delacroix, and the courtyard of the Hôtel de la Marine.

If you’re missing some of the program’s former landmarks, there are, at least, sizable artworks in Paris that are not officially a part of the “Hors le murs” program. At Saint-Eustache, there’s work by Rémi Marcel, winner of the sixth Rubis Mécénat Prize, who presents two half-columns—one made of clay with wheat seeds that evoke growth and renewal, and the other of plaster, suggesting the cycle of life. At the Musée d’Orsay, there’s Jenny Holzer’s text projections, which illuminate the facade of the former railway station at night and feature words from its archives.

Given the cloudy weather on Wednesday, the concentration of fair-associated works around the Grand Palais was not necessarily a disadvantage. Still, a few visitors could be heard commenting on the program’s relatively subdued palette, which, apart from Yinka Shonibare’s and Keita Miyazaki’s vibrantly hued works, is dominated by black, brown, and gray.

Among the super-VIPs arriving at the Grand Palais for Art Basel’s invitation-only event held ahead of Thursday’s 10 a.m. preview, there were also concerns about the security of the artworks, since they were set against the backdrop of the unrest that followed protests on October 17. None appear to have been damaged since going on view, however. (Later, Kwade clarified on Instagram that her piece would eventually be removed for fear of future damage.)

The Public Program runs from October 21 to 25. Visitors can explore it independently or seek out the École du Louvre students stationed at the participating venues, where they are available to share insights into the works on view. “The docents are not out-of-touch students, disconnected from contemporary art or today’s social struggles,” said Laure Saffroy-Lepesqueur, an instructor involved in the partnership between Art Basel and the École du Louvre. “They volunteer their time to make artworks more accessible and understandable beyond the purely commercial framework of the art fair, striving to deepen our understanding of the artists’ aesthetic, political, social, and poetic thinking.” So, go ahead and talk to them!

Palais d’Iéna x Alice Diop Image Credit: Courtesy Miu Miu When Art Basel Paris was created five years ago, its original name, Paris+ by Art Basel, featured a plus sign that promised a broader, more multidisciplinary vision of what the fair could be. Though that ambition still hasn’t been entirely fulfilled, the Palais d’Iéna continues to embody it through its partnership with Miu Miu, returning for the third year as official partner of the fair’s Public Program. This year, French filmmaker Alice Diop (b. 1979) takes over the monumental concrete building with Geste de Consolation , an immersive project weaving together film, photography, sculpture, poetry, dance, and music. Diop explores how images have shaped representations of Black women, and how art might offer a form of repair. From a black-and-white photographic self-portrait by South African artist Zanele Muholi, who lies naked on a bed holding a round mirror before their face, to Simone Leigh’s totemic Sentinel (Mami Wata) , described as “[her] interpretation of a West African desert spirit, a deity who has destructive powers, as well as creative-generative ones,” the exhibition unfolds as a journey through Diop’s visual memory. Her own two-screen film installation is, in her words, an “intimate visual scrapbook of images of Black women that haunt [her].” A library and living room with seating recycled from Miu Miu’s latest Paris fashion show offer a space for thought and learning, turning the Palais into a setting for reflection and collective consolation.

Petit Palais x Cosima von Bonin Image Credit: Courtesy Art Basel In front of the Petit Palais, there’s a Corten steel sculpture merging the body of a pregnant woman with the hull of a ship is not part of the Public Program. It’s the starting point of Prune Nourry’s carte blanche, which extends into the museum. But its entrance has been taken over by a work that is a part of the Public Program: a pack of leather octopuses, mohair whales, and velvet St. Bernards. This playful menagerie was commissioned by Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez for the Loewe Fall/Winter 2026 show. It is the work of German artist Cosima von Bonin (b. 1962). With their soft bodies and cartoonish expressions, the oversized creatures unsettle the distinction between high art and popular culture, challenging what a museum might consider worthy of attention. Their apparent inability to serve a functional purpose also offers a humorous counterpoint to a culture obsessed with productivity and achievement.

Trocadéro x Tracey Emin Image Credit: Courtesy Art Basel This year, the Parvis des Droits de l’Homme takes center stage, stepping in for the Place Vendôme, which traditionally acts as a showcase for monumental art installations. With three imposing bronze sculptures, Tracey Emin (b. 1963) has transformed this long-standing tourist hotspot, now a favourite backdrop for influencers thanks to its spectacular Eiffel Tower view, into a meditation on the female body. One figure lies stretched across the ground, another kneels with her legs apart, while the third sits upright on a rock, her face veiled. Their unguarded poses evoke isolation, emotional fragility, and the strength it takes to endure; their roughly modelled surfaces give them a raw, intimate quality.

Jardin de la Nouvelle-France x Boz Deseo Garden Image Credit: Courtesy Art Basel In the Jardin de la Nouvelle-France, busts of French explorers Jacques Cartier and Samuel de Champlain uncritically commemorate Canada’s colonial past. Los Angeles-based artist Boz Deseo Garden (b. 1997) challenges that legacy with two slender bronze lightning rods. One, dated 1798, recalls the case of Charlotte, an enslaved woman in Montreal whose escape led a judge to order her release; the other, dated 1834, marks the abolition of slavery across most of the British Empire. Titled Celia, or the Misfortunes of Virtue (2026), the installation also invokes the Marquis de Sade’s novel Justine, or the Misfortunes of Virtue , whose heroine is struck by lightning.

Square Jean Perrin x Lionel Sabatté Image Credit: Courtesy Art Basel A flock of birds perches atop uneven columns in front of the Grand Palais, their silhouettes rising against the surrounding architecture. Living descendants of dinosaurs and witnesses to an ancient evolutionary history, birds are a recurring motif in the work of Lionel Sabatté (b. 1975), a finalist for the 2025 Prix Marcel Duchamp. The artist explores transformation through unconventional materials, including dust, metal, and volcanic stone, tracing how living things change over time. For Champs d’oiseaux (2026), he transformed foundry waste into totem-like sculptures whose rough surfaces evoke tree bark. His raptors and owls, each with empty eye sockets, suggest inward vision and nocturnal perception. Their precarious balance evokes migration, as though they have paused before taking flight again. Accidental rainbow hues reveal the unexpected beauty of industrial materials.

Chapelle des Petits-Augustins x Kutluğ Ataman Image Credit: Courtesy Art Basel Forty television screens and an equal number of mismatched seats, varying in size and shape, fill the Chapelle des Petits-Augustins. The cacophony of voices and images is disorienting, yet strangely compelling. You will want to sit down and watch, drawn into the fragments of lives unfolding around you. In Küba (2004), Turkish artist Kutluğ Ataman (b. 1961) brings together the testimonies of 40 residents of a now-vanished settlement on the outskirts of Istanbul, founded in the late 1960s by people fleeing political persecution. Each person shares their memories, fears, beliefs and dreams. Heard simultaneously, their stories overlap without any single voice taking precedence. Gradually, a collective portrait emerges, revealing a community shaped by migration, poverty, solidarity and survival. Viewed in sequence, the testimonies amount to 28 hours of footage, making the work almost impossible to watch in its entirety. “By choosing which television to watch and which individual to follow, the viewer becomes an editor of the installation,” a docent-student from the École du Louvre told ARTnews .
excerpt_original: Despite so much grayish art, these monumental works still offer plenty of pleasure.

article_text:
While directing the comedy-horror film “ Christmas at the Kringles ,” Kevin Lewis found himself filled with a holly jolly spirit.

“When I was shooting some of these scenes, it was so hard for me not to mess them up because I was busting a gut,” he says. “I remember thinking, ‘Gosh, you should do some more comedies,’ because every day I would finish shooting and I’d be happy.”

Netflix Touts International Success Amid Content Leadership Shake-Up, Eyes More Broadcaster Deals After TF1 and Globo Pacts

It’s no surprise that Lewis, a prolific filmmaker who often keeps both feet in the horror realm with features like 2022’s “The Accursed” and last year’s “Pig Hill,” was cracking up on set. “Kringles” stars a gaggle of comic actors, including Ron Livingston, Rachel Bilson, Rob Riggle, Thomas Lennon, Donald Faison, David Wain and Beverly D’Angelo. The film, scripted by Zack Imbrogno and in theaters Friday via Briarcliff Entertainment, concerns a dad, Mark (Livingston), who moves his family next door to a patriarch, Nick (Lennon), who takes Christmas very seriously and has some sinister intentions.

Part of the reason Lewis was initially interested in the script was recalling a neighborhood dad who reminded him of the overzealous Nick.

“I used to have a neighbor, I nicknamed him ‘Father of the Year,’” Lewis says. “He had two girls and he’d come out and decorate the house with the lights and stuff, and he’d put out ramps in the street and have his girls hop with their bikes and do all this crazy stuff. I was like, ‘Father of the Year is at it again,’ but I felt like it was performative. He wanted everyone to see what he was doing, but he really wasn’t doing it because he liked to do it. When I got that script, these things started flooding in.”

From there, the comedy deepened with the game cast, who have enough collective chops to improvise laugh-out-loud moments.

“I work in a way where the script’s an organic thing,” Lewis says. “It’s always evolving. When you’re shooting it, it’s not exactly what was on the page. Whether it’s time constraints, budget or things just change — you have different ideas. For me, meeting with these actors, we all knew the through-line of the narrative we were going toward. But we could take detours a little bit, and boy, we did. Those actors are so quick-witted and fast on their feet. Every take was different.”

Also, the director says the comedy on set allowed him to calibrate the perfect blend of horror and laughs in the finished product.

“When I’m shooting, it’s like I’m collecting clay,” he says. “When I’m finished, I’m going to cut the movie and I’m going to decide where I’m going to put that clay. I always knew that I didn’t want the tone to be too grotesque, and neither did the actors. That was one of the first questions Ron asked me was about the tone of the movie. I said, ‘Like “Beetlejuice,” comic book horror.’ This wasn’t ‘Terrifier.’ I’m not looking for a kill count. And that’s cool, those movies are their own thing. But that wasn’t this.”

Beyond the laughs and blood, Lewis also was touched by some of the emotional beats baked into the script.

“I liked the father and son through-line in this film,” he says. “As crazy as it is, there is a good theme about being present in one’s life and not trying to just keep pushing forward. You should enjoy the moment, seize the day and enjoy what you have right now. I really like that theme of ‘Kringles.’ I really tapped into the father being kind of aloof, because I’m always thinking about my filmmaking career. I’ve got kids and I have to be present for them, right? That always brought me back. So I worked on that on this movie. At the end of the day, it’s just going through life.”

Ultimately, Lewis valued the teamwork of shooting “Kringles.”

“I just like working, man,” he says. “I like meeting cool people and getting together and telling stories.”

article_text:
Creatures, fairies and dark hunters: fantastical fun at Melbourne’s Starfall ball – in pictures

Fantasy fiction fans stepped into a make-believe world at the Melbourne Town Hall on 24 October for the Celestial Events Starfall ball. Tiaras, pixie ears, horns and wings proved popular attire for the immersive event inspired by fantasy novel writers such as Sarah J Maas and Rebecca Yarros

Mridula Amin

Sun 25 Oct 2026 10.00 EDT

title_original: Documenta 16, quattro nuovi ingressi nel team curatoriale guidato da Naomi Beckwith
editorial_title_zh: 第16届文献展，内奥米·贝克with（Naomi Beckwith）领导的策展团队迎来四位新成员
editorial_excerpt_zh: 雷文·查孔（Raven Chacon）、奥塞·邦苏（Osei Bonsu）、蒂梅亚·容豪斯（Timea Junghaus）和诺姆·西加尔（Noam Segal）加入正在为该展会下一届筹备的工作小组，展会计划于2027年在卡塞尔举行 本文《第16届文献展，内奥米·贝克with（Naomi Beckwith）领导的策展团队迎来四位新成员》来源于……
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "关于充满波折的第16届文献展的讨论仍在继续。这场每五年在德国卡塞尔举办一次、专注于当代艺术的国际盛会迎来了四位新成员加入其策展团队。距离定于2027年6月12日至9月19日开幕不到八个月之际，艺术总监内奥米·贝克with（Naomi Beckwith）正式宣布，雷文·查孔（Raven Chacon）将作为独立策展人加入，奥塞·邦苏（Osei Bonsu）、蒂梅亚·容豪斯（Timea Junghaus）和诺姆·西加尔（Noam Segal）将作为策展顾问加入。这四位新成员将与由卡拉·阿塞韦多-耶茨（Carla Acevedo-Yates）、罗米·克劳福德（Romi Crawford）、梅拉·A·罗德里格斯·卡斯特罗（Mayra A. Rodríguez Castro）和翁笑雨（Xiaoyu Weng）已经组成的团队并肩工作，共同敲定展会的节目单与艺术方向。", "links": [{"text": "turbolenta edizione", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/arte-contemporanea/documenta-16-alcuni-artisti-rifiutano-di-partecipare-per-le-posizioni-della-germania-su-gaza/"}, {"text": "documenta 16", "url": "https://documenta.de/en"}, {"text": "manifestazione", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/tag/documenta/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "新策展人都是谁", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在宣布的名字中，雷文·查孔格外引人注目，他是一位作曲家、表演者和视觉艺术家，出生于纳瓦霍族领地内的堡垒Defiance。2022年，他凭借作品《无声弥撒》（Voiceless Mass）成为首位荣获普利策音乐奖的本土原住民艺术家。他的实践横跨实验音乐、装置与表演。2009年至2018年，他曾是Postcommodity集体成员之一，并随该集体参加了第14届文献展以及卡耐基国际艺术展（Carnegie International）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该团体完成的项目还包括《驱避围栏》（Repellent Fence），这是一个长约三公里半的大地艺术装置，构想沿美国与墨西哥边境展开。此外，查孔还致力于面向年轻原住民一代的音乐教育活动：自2004年起，他一直参与美洲原住民作曲家学徒项目（Native American Composer Apprenticeship Project），通过该项目指导了三百多位年轻作曲家创作弦乐四重奏的新总谱。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/d16_cd_2026_09_18_photo_nicolas_wefers_007_mid-1024x-1024x768.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "第16届文献展海报，2026年，© Design Commons, documenta und Museum Fridericianum gGmbH, 摄影：尼古拉斯·韦弗斯（Nicolas Wefers）", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "与他一同加入团队的还有奥塞·邦苏，他是一位英国加纳裔策展人和艺术史学家，目前担任伦敦泰特现代美术馆国际艺术、非洲与侨民部高级策展人（Jorge M. Pérez Senior Curator of International Art, Africa, and Diaspora）。他的工作聚焦于艺术史书写的后殖民视角，以及全球与跨国现代主义的形式，并对非洲及全球南方的艺术家给予了特别关注。在泰特美术馆期间，他通过藏品收购和展览项目，为致力于非洲及侨民艺术收藏的发展作出了贡献。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "艺术史学家兼策展人蒂梅亚·容豪斯则为团队带来了在罗姆人和辛提人当代艺术领域的丰富经验。她曾担任柏林欧洲罗姆人艺术与文化研究所的创所总监，任期自2017年至2025年，并在2007年策划了第52届威尼斯双年展上的首个罗姆人国家馆《失去的天堂》（Paradise Lost）。她的研究涉及移民、社区流离失所及当代技术转型等议题，并对人工智能的影响给予了特别关注。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "诺姆·西加尔完成了团队的组建，她是一位策展人兼学者，主要研究当代艺术、科技与社会之间的交汇点。她目前担任纽约所罗门·R·古根海姆美术馆的LG电子副策展人（LG Electronics Associate Curator），并在该馆负责LG古根海姆奖。在她的职业生涯中，她曾与东京宫、国立网球场现代美术馆、Performa、里沃利城堡、光州双年展以及柏林双年展等国际机构和活动展开合作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "第16届文献展与内奥米·贝克with宣布的方向", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该团队的扩充契合了内奥米·贝克with为第十六届展会所勾勒的研究方向，旨在探索将即兴创作作为一种应对不确定性以及审视当代科技承诺与风险的工具的可能性。其明确的目标是构建一个跨文化实验与对话的空间，在此空间中，艺术实践与集体学习形式能够共同助力，去想象在充斥着不稳定与转型的世界中和平共处的新可能。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我非常高兴能与这些杰出的艺术家和学者合作，他们的信念与他们对合作实践的承诺一样坚定，”贝克with在介绍新成员时说道。", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Si continua a parlare della turbolenta edizione di documenta 16 . Quattro nuovi ingressi nel gruppo curatoriale della manifestazione internazionale dedicata all’arte contemporanea che si svolge ogni cinque anni a Kassel, in Germania. A meno di otto mesi dall’apertura, in programma dal 12 giugno al 19 settembre 2027, la direttrice artistica Naomi Beckwith ha infatti annunciato l’ingresso di Raven Chacon come curatrice indipendente e di Osei Bonsu , Timea Junghaus e Noam Segal come consulenti curatoriali. Le quattro figure si affiancheranno al gruppo già composto da Carla Acevedo-Yates , Romi Crawford , Mayra A . Rodríguez Castro e Xiaoyu Weng , contribuendo alla definizione del programma e dell’orientamento artistico della manifestazione.", "links": [{"text": "turbolenta edizione", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/arte-contemporanea/documenta-16-alcuni-artisti-rifiutano-di-partecipare-per-le-posizioni-della-germania-su-gaza/"}, {"text": "documenta 16", "url": "https://documenta.de/en"}, {"text": "manifestazione", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/tag/documenta/"}]}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Chi sono i nuovi curatori"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Tra i nomi annunciati spicca quello di Raven Chacon, compositore, performer e artista visivo nato a Fort Defiance, nel territorio della Navajo Nation. Nel 2022 è stato il primo artista indigeno a ricevere il Pulitzer Prize for Music con la composizione Voiceless Mass . La sua pratica attraversa musica sperimentale, installazione e performance. Dal 2009 al 2018 ha fatto parte del collettivo Postcommodity, con cui ha partecipato a documenta 14 e alla Carnegie International."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Tra i progetti realizzati dal gruppo figura anche Repellent Fence , un’installazione di land art lunga circa tre chilometri e mezzo, concepita lungo il confine tra Stati Uniti e Messico. Chacon è inoltre impegnato in attività di formazione musicale rivolte alle giovani generazioni indigene: dal 2004 partecipa al Native American Composer Apprenticeship Project, attraverso il quale ha accompagnato oltre trecento giovani compositori nella realizzazione di nuove partiture per quartetto d’archi."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/d16_cd_2026_09_18_photo_nicolas_wefers_007_mid-1024x-1024x768.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Poster del D16, 2026, © Design Commons, documenta und Museum Fridericianum gGmbH, Foto: Nicolas Wefers", "credit": "Exibart"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Accanto a lui entra nel gruppo Osei Bonsu, curatore e storico dell’arte britannico-ghanese, attualmente Jorge M. Pérez Senior Curator of International Art, Africa, and Diaspora alla Tate Modern di Londra. Il suo lavoro si concentra sulle prospettive postcoloniali della storiografia artistica e sulle forme di modernismo globale e transnazionale, con particolare attenzione agli artisti africani e del Sud globale. Alla Tate ha contribuito allo sviluppo della collezione dedicata all’arte africana e della diaspora, attraverso acquisizioni e progetti espositivi."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Timea Junghaus, storica dell’arte e curatrice, porta invece nel gruppo una lunga esperienza nel campo dell’arte contemporanea rom e sinti. È stata direttrice fondatrice dell’European Roma Institute for Arts and Culture di Berlino, incarico ricoperto dal 2017 al 2025, e nel 2007 ha curato Paradise Lost , primo Padiglione Rom alla 52ª Biennale di Venezia. article_text:
Si continua a parlare della turbolenta edizione di documenta 16 . Quattro nuovi ingressi nel gruppo curatoriale della manifestazione internazionale dedicata all’arte contemporanea che si svolge ogni cinque anni a Kassel, in Germania. A meno di otto mesi dall’apertura, in programma dal 12 giugno al 19 settembre 2027, la direttrice artistica Naomi Beckwith ha infatti annunciato l’ingresso di Raven Chacon come curatrice indipendente e di Osei Bonsu , Timea Junghaus e Noam Segal come consulenti curatoriali. Le quattro figure si affiancheranno al gruppo già composto da Carla Acevedo-Yates , Romi Crawford , Mayra A . Rodríguez Castro e Xiaoyu Weng , contribuendo alla definizione del programma e dell’orientamento artistico della manifestazione.

Chi sono i nuovi curatori

Tra i nomi annunciati spicca quello di Raven Chacon, compositore, performer e artista visivo nato a Fort Defiance, nel territorio della Navajo Nation. Nel 2022 è stato il primo artista indigeno a ricevere il Pulitzer Prize for Music con la composizione Voiceless Mass . La sua pratica attraversa musica sperimentale, installazione e performance. Dal 2009 al 2018 ha fatto parte del collettivo Postcommodity, con cui ha partecipato a documenta 14 e alla Carnegie International.

Tra i progetti realizzati dal gruppo figura anche Repellent Fence , un’installazione di land art lunga circa tre chilometri e mezzo, concepita lungo il confine tra Stati Uniti e Messico. Chacon è inoltre impegnato in attività di formazione musicale rivolte alle giovani generazioni indigene: dal 2004 partecipa al Native American Composer Apprenticeship Project, attraverso il quale ha accompagnato oltre trecento giovani compositori nella realizzazione di nuove partiture per quartetto d’archi.

Accanto a lui entra nel gruppo Osei Bonsu, curatore e storico dell’arte britannico-ghanese, attualmente Jorge M. Pérez Senior Curator of International Art, Africa, and Diaspora alla Tate Modern di Londra. Il suo lavoro si concentra sulle prospettive postcoloniali della storiografia artistica e sulle forme di modernismo globale e transnazionale, con particolare attenzione agli artisti africani e del Sud globale. Alla Tate ha contribuito allo sviluppo della collezione dedicata all’arte africana e della diaspora, attraverso acquisizioni e progetti espositivi.

Timea Junghaus, storica dell’arte e curatrice, porta invece nel gruppo una lunga esperienza nel campo dell’arte contemporanea rom e sinti. È stata direttrice fondatrice dell’European Roma Institute for Arts and Culture di Berlino, incarico ricoperto dal 2017 al 2025, e nel 2007 ha curato Paradise Lost , primo Padiglione Rom alla 52ª Biennale di Venezia. La sua ricerca affronta questioni legate alla migrazione, allo spostamento delle comunità e alle trasformazioni tecnologiche contemporanee, con particolare attenzione alle implicazioni dell’intelligenza artificiale.

Completa il gruppo Noam Segal, curatrice e studiosa che si occupa delle intersezioni tra arte contemporanea, tecnologia e società. Attualmente ricopre il ruolo di LG Electronics Associate Curator al Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum di New York, dove si occupa anche del LG Guggenheim Award. Nel corso della sua attività ha collaborato con istituzioni e manifestazioni internazionali come Palais de Tokyo, Jeu de Paume, Performa, Castello di Rivoli, Gwangju Biennale e Berlin Biennale.

Documenta 16 e la direzione annunciata da Naomi Beckwith

L’ampliamento del gruppo si inserisce nella direzione di ricerca delineata da Naomi Beckwith per la sedicesima edizione, che intende esplorare le possibilità dell’improvvisazione come strumento per confrontarsi con l’incertezza e interrogare le promesse e i rischi delle tecnologie contemporanee. L’obiettivo dichiarato è quello di costruire uno spazio di sperimentazione e dialogo transculturale, nel quale pratiche artistiche e forme di apprendimento collettivo possano contribuire a immaginare nuove possibilità di convivenza in un mondo attraversato da instabilità e trasformazioni.

«Non potrei essere più entusiasta di lavorare con questi straordinari artisti e studiosi, le cui convinzioni sono forti quanto il loro impegno nella pratica collaborativa», ha dichiarato Beckwith presentando i nuovi componenti.
